questions.question: What are the main classes of biomolecules? Give one function each.
questions.solution:
**Carbohydrates:** Energy source (glucose, starch)
**Proteins:** Enzymes and structural components (hemoglobin, collagen)
**Lipids:** Energy storage and membrane structure (fats, phospholipids)
**Nucleic acids:** Genetic information (DNA, RNA)
questions.knowledgeNote: Biomolecules are essential for life. Carbohydrates = (CH₂O)n; Proteins = polymers of amino acids.

questions.question: Differentiate between DNA and RNA on the basis of sugar, strands, bases, stability and function.
questions.solution:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) are both nucleic acids made of nucleotides, but they differ as follows:

| Basis | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| **Sugar** | **Deoxyribose** (one less oxygen) | **Ribose** |
| **Strands** | **Double stranded**, two antiparallel polynucleotide chains held by hydrogen bonds | Usually **single stranded**; folds on itself |
| **Bases** | A, G, C and **T (thymine)**; A = T and G = C (Chargaff's rule) | A, G, C and **U (uracil)** in place of T |
| **Stability** | More **chemically stable** (no 2'–OH group) — ideal for long-term storage of heredity | **Less stable**, is rapidly degraded — suited to short-term information transfer |
| **Location** | Mainly in the **nucleus** (nucleoid in prokaryotes); also in mitochondria and chloroplasts | In the nucleus **and cytoplasm** |
| **Function** | The **genetic material**; stores hereditary information, replicates it and serves as the template for transcription | **mRNA** carries the message to ribosomes, **tRNA** carries amino acids, **rRNA** is a structural part of the ribosome; some RNAs are the genetic material of viruses |

**Extra point:** both are made of a nucleotide = pentose sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base, and are linked by **3'–5' phosphodiester bonds**.
questions.knowledgeNote: DNA has deoxyribose, is double stranded and uses thymine, making it stable; RNA has ribose, is single stranded and uses uracil.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a nucleotide and explain its role in DNA.
questions.solution:
A **nucleotide** consists of: (1) a pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), (2) a nitrogenous base (A,T,G,C in DNA), (3) a phosphate group.

In DNA, nucleotides form a double helix via complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C) connected by hydrogen bonds.
questions.knowledgeNote: DNA = deoxyribonucleic acid; RNA = ribonucleic acid. DNA stores genetic info; RNA transfers it.

questions.question: Explain how temperature and pH affect enzyme activity, and state the advantage of using immobilised enzymes in industry.
questions.solution:
**Enzymes** are biological catalysts — mostly proteins — that speed up reactions by lowering the **activation energy** without being used up.

**Effect of temperature**
- As temperature rises, molecules gain kinetic energy and the **rate of reaction increases** up to an **optimum temperature**.
- Above the optimum, the weak bonds maintaining the enzyme's tertiary structure break and the enzyme is **denatured**, so the active site loses its shape and the **rate falls to zero**. The enzyme molecule is not consumed, it is permanently changed.
- Optimum is about **37 °C** for most human enzymes, but the thermophilic bacterium *Thermus aquaticus* gives **Taq DNA polymerase** with an optimum near **72 °C** that stays active at 95 °C — the basis of **PCR**.

**Effect of pH**
- Every enzyme has an **optimum pH** at which the ionisation of the amino acids of its active site is correct for substrate binding.
- **Pepsin** works best at about **pH 2** (stomach), **trypsin** at about **pH 8–9** (small intestine) and **salivary amylase** at about **pH 6.7–7**.
- A shift in pH changes the charges on the active site and on the substrate, so the enzyme–substrate complex fails to form and activity drops; extreme pH also denatures the enzyme.

**Advantage of immobilised enzymes**
- Enzymes are bound to an **insoluble inert support** such as **calcium alginate beads**, DEAE-cellulose or acrylamide gel.
- They can then be **reused many times**, are **more stable** to heat and pH, and the **product can be separated easily** from the enzyme, allowing continuous flow operation and reducing cost — e.g. **lactase** to make lactose-free milk, **glucose isomerase** to convert glucose syrup into fructose syrup, and **urease** in urea-based biogas plants.
questions.knowledgeNote: Every enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; immobilised enzymes are reusable and make product separation easy.

questions.question: Differentiate between habitat and ecological niche with suitable examples.
questions.solution:
**Habitat** and **ecological niche** are two different but related terms.

**Habitat:** The natural place where an organism lives. It is a *physical place* and is described mainly by the **abiotic** conditions prevailing there — light, temperature, water, air, soil and shelter.

**Ecological niche:** The total set of **biotic and abiotic** conditions within which an organism lives, together with the **functional role** it plays in that community — i.e. *what it eats, when it feeds, where it feeds and how it interacts with neighbours*.

| Basis | Habitat | Ecological niche |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | A place of occurrence | A functional role plus total conditions |
| Factors | Mainly abiotic | Both biotic and abiotic |
| Number for a species | Usually one | A species may occupy several niches |
| Question answered | *Where does it live?* | *Where, when, how and on what does it live?* |

**Example:** A toad (*Bufo*) lives in a **pond**, so its habitat is the pond. But it feeds at night on insects and insects of that pond, so its **niche** is *nocturnal insectivore living at the edge of a freshwater pond*.

**Another example:** The starling bird lives in the same **habitat** (a building and its lawn) in every season, but its **niche** changes with the season — insectivore in summer, grain eater in winter.
questions.knowledgeNote: Habitat is the place where an organism lives; niche is the role it plays plus the biotic and abiotic conditions it needs.

questions.question: A desert plant develops a thick cuticle, leaves reduced to spines and sunken stomata. Such inherited modifications are called — (a) acclimatization (b) adaptation (c) acclimation (d) mutation
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (b) adaptation**

**Reasoning:**
- An **adaptation** is an inherited (genetic) structural or functional feature that has been shaped by natural selection over many generations and helps the organism survive in its environment. Thick cuticle, spines instead of leaves (as in *Opuntia*) and sunken stomata (as in *Nerium* and *Cycas*) are **morphological adaptations** to conserve water in arid conditions. ✔
- **Acclimatization / acclimation** is a temporary, non-genetic physiological adjustment made by an individual organism in response to a change in the environment — for example, a person sweating more in hot weather. ✘
- A **mutation** is a sudden heritable change in a gene or chromosome; the changes given here are coordinated, useful modifications, not random mutations. ✘

Hence the correct answer is **(b) adaptation**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Adaptations are inherited and genetically fixed; acclimatization is a temporary, non-genetic adjustment by the individual.

questions.question: Describe any four types of interspecific relationships found between organisms, giving one example of each.
questions.solution:
Two different species living close together usually interact. The nature and effect of the interaction is called an **interspecific relationship**. Four important types are:

**1. Mutualism (+, +)** — both partners are *benefited*; it is **obligate or facultative**.
- *Rhizobium* bacteria living in the root nodules of soybean (*Glycine max*) get shelter and food; the plant gets nitrogen fixed into usable form.
- Mycorrhizal association of fungal hyphae (e.g. *Russula*) with the roots of pine (*Pinus*).
- Fig tree (*Ficus*) and its pollinating fig-wasp (*Blastophaga*).

**2. Commensalism (+, 0)** — one partner is *benefited*, the other is *neither benefited nor harmed*.
- Cattle egret (*Bubalus coromanda*) following grazing cattle to pick up insects and seeds disturbed from the grass; the cattle are unaffected.
- Orchid (*Vanda*) epiphyte growing on the branch of a mango tree — it gets support and better light, the mango is neither helped nor harmed.

**3. Parasitism (+, −)** — the **parasite** benefits and the **host** is harmed; the parasite is small and lives *on or inside* the host.
- *Ascaris lumbricoides* in the intestine of man; tapeworm (*Taenia*) in the human gut.
- *Rafflesia* on the stem of *Tetrastigma* vine.
- *Puccinia graminis* causing wheat rust; *Cuscuta* (dodder) on a mustard plant.

**4. Competition (−, −)** — both partners are *harmed* because the limited resource (food, space, light) is limited and they compete for it.
- *Paramecium caudatum* and *Paramecium aurelia* in the same culture — in Gause's experiment both declined when grown together.
- Two crop plants of different species sown in the same field competing for light, water and minerals.

**5. Amensalism (0, −)** and **Predation (+, −)** may also be listed: *Penicillium* fungus secreting penicillin that kills competing bacteria is amensalism; a dragonfly (*Crocothemis*) eating a grasshopper is predation.
questions.knowledgeNote: Mutualism benefits both, commensalism benefits one, parasitism benefits one and harms the other, competition harms both partners.

questions.question: Explain the role of decomposers in an ecosystem with two examples.
questions.solution:
**Decomposers** are organisms that break down complex dead organic matter (cadavers, leaf litter, faeces and wastes) into simple **inorganic** substances by secreting extracellular digestive enzymes.

**Roles in an ecosystem:**
1. They recycle nutrients — carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and mineral salts locked in dead bodies are returned to the soil and water as CO₂, H₂O, NH₃ and mineral salts.
2. They maintain **soil fertility** and keep the **nutrient cycle** turning; without them nutrients would remain locked and the ecosystem would collapse.
3. They remove dead bodies from the environment (sanitation) and help clean up pollution.

**Examples:**
1. Saprophytes — fungi such as *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, *Penicillium* and *Agaricus*, and saprophytic bacteria such as *Bacillus*, which digest cellulose and lignin of fallen leaves and wood.
2. Symbionts — cellulose-digesting bacteria and flagellates (*Trichonympha*) living in the rumen of cow and in the gut of termites, which enable those animals to use grass and wood as food.
questions.knowledgeNote: Decomposers convert dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients, so without them the nutrient cycle of an ecosystem would stop.

questions.question: What is biodiversity? Explain the levels of biodiversity and their significance.
questions.solution:
**Biodiversity:** Variety of life at all levels.

**Levels:**
1. **Genetic diversity** — variation within species (crop varieties, breeds)
2. **Species diversity** — number and abundance of species
3. **Ecosystem diversity** — variety of habitats and ecological processes

**Significance:** Ecosystem stability, resource provision (food, medicine), cultural value.
questions.knowledgeNote: Nepal has 44 protected areas. Chitwan National Park (UNESCO site) is a biodiversity hotspot.

questions.question: Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ conservation of biodiversity with two examples of each.
questions.solution:
**In-situ conservation**
- Conservation of species **in their own natural habitat**, with all their normal ecological interactions intact.
- **Examples:**
 1. **National parks and conservation areas** — Sagarmatha National Park (Solukhumbu), Chitwan National Park, Bardiya National Park.
 2. **Community forests** managed by Community Forestry User Groups (CFUGs) and **sacred groves** such as the Bhuwan Patwari grove in Uttarakhand.
- **Advantage:** preserves the whole ecosystem, its food webs and gene pool, and is economical and self-sustaining.

**Ex-situ conservation**
- Removal of species from their natural habitat and **maintenance outside it** under controlled conditions.
- **Examples:**
 1. **Zoos** — the Central Zoo, Kathmandu, and **aquaria** for fish and aquatic animals.
 2. **Botanical gardens and seed banks** — the Godawari Botanical Garden and Lalitpur, the National Herbarium and Plant Laboratories (with a seed bank) at Godawari.
- **Advantage:** rescues species whose habitat is already destroyed, allows controlled breeding and re-introduction, and keeps genetic material for future use.
- **Limitation:** costly; captive individuals lose natural behaviour, feeding on natural food and inter-specific relationships.

**Conclusion:** In-situ conservation is always preferable, but where the habitat has already shrunk, ex-situ measures act as a **last line of defence**; the two are best used together.
questions.knowledgeNote: In-situ conservation keeps species in their natural habitat; ex-situ keeps them in zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and aquaria.

questions.question: Describe any five threats to biodiversity in Nepal and state one suitable conservation measure against each.
questions.solution:
Nepal harbours a rich biodiversity (over 118 ecosystems, 284 plant species of high value) but it faces serious threats.

1. **Habitat destruction and fragmentation** — conversion of Terai forest to farmland, urbanization, road and irrigation development, encroachment on the Terai arcs.
   **Measure:** declare and strictly enforce protected areas (national parks, conservation areas), expand community forestry, and grow **agroforestry** and shelterbelts on farmland.

2. **Over-grazing and forest degradation** — free grazing of cattle in national parks, cutting of fuelwood and timber beyond regeneration.
   **Measure:** **rotational and controlled grazing**, stall-feeding with fodder crops, silvipasture development, and management of forests by user groups under the Forest Act.

3. **Illegal hunting, poaching and wildlife trade** — killing of rhinoceros for horn, tiger for skin and bones, snow leopard, musk deer and many birds for the illegal feather and ivory trade.
   **Measure:** strong anti-poaching patrols, enforcement of the hunting ban, community-based anti-poaching units, reward schemes, and compliance with **CITES**; Nepal has a very good record in fighting the ivory and rhino-horn rackets.

4. **Over-exploitation of non-timber forest products (NTFP)** — unsustainable collection of medicinal and aromatic plants such as *Taxus* (yew), *Paris polyphylla* and *Nardostachys jatamansi*, and of edible fungi, seeds and resins.
   **Measure:** licensing and quota systems for collection, controlled harvest in their natural habitat, and **cultivation of threatened species** in community nurseries.

5. **Invasive alien species** — *Lantana camara*, *Mimosa diplotricha* and crofton weed (*Ageratina adenophora*) invade forest edges, block regeneration and cause heavy leaf fall in the middle hills.
   **Measure:** early detection, manual and chemical control, and public awareness programmes; strict phytosanitary checks to prevent new introductions.

6. **Pollution and climate change** — industrial effluents, solid waste and rivers polluted by untreated sewage, plus river-training works that cut off spawning grounds of mahseer and gharial.
   **Measure:** environmental impact assessment before projects, sewage treatment, river conservation programmes, and emission-reduction measures.
questions.knowledgeNote: Nepal's chief biodiversity threats are habitat destruction, over-grazing, poaching, over-exploitation, invasive species and pollution.

questions.question: Define ecosystem. Describe the structure of an ecosystem with a diagram.
questions.solution:
**Ecosystem:** A community of organisms interacting with their physical environment.

**Structure:**
- **Abiotic:** Temperature, light, water, soil, nutrients
- **Biotic:** Producers (plants), Consumers (herbivores, carnivores), Decomposers (bacteria, fungi)

Trophic levels: Producers → Primary consumers → Secondary consumers → Tertiary consumers
Decomposers recycle nutrients from all levels.
questions.knowledgeNote: Energy flows one-way in ecosystems (10% rule); nutrients cycle.

questions.question: Differentiate between the pyramid of numbers and the pyramid of biomass, and state one case in which each becomes inverted.
questions.solution:
**Pyramid of numbers** shows the **number of individual organisms** present at each successive trophic level.
- It **depends on the size of the organism**, so its shape changes with the ecosystem.
- In a **grassland** it is **upright**: grass (many) → grasshopper (fewer) → frog (few) → snake (fewest).
- In a **tree ecosystem** it becomes **spindle-shaped**: one huge banyan tree → many herbivorous insects → a few insectivorous birds → a few hawks.
- In a **parasitic food chain** it is **completely inverted**: a single tree → one *Mistletoe* → several lice → millions of bacteria.

**Pyramid of biomass** shows the **standing crop (dry mass)** of living material at each trophic level, usually in g m⁻² or kg m⁻².
- It is **always upright in terrestrial ecosystems** because the mass of each trophic level is less than the level below it.
- It becomes **inverted in an aquatic ecosystem**: phytoplankton (very small standing crop) → zooplankton (larger) → small fish → large fish, because the phytoplankton reproduce and are eaten so rapidly that their **turnover rate is very high**, so their standing crop at any instant is small.
- In a grassland plot the biomass of insects and earthworms may exceed that of the grass, giving a partly upright or spindle-shaped pyramid.

**Contrast:** the pyramid of numbers counts individuals, whereas the pyramid of biomass measures total living mass; only the pyramid of energy is always upright.
questions.knowledgeNote: Pyramid of numbers can invert in a tree ecosystem; pyramid of biomass can invert in water because phytoplankton have a very high turnover rate.

questions.question: What is ecological succession? Explain with the example of xerosere.
questions.solution:
**Ecological succession:** Gradual change in species composition of a community over time.

**Xerosere** (dry habitat succession):
Lichen → Moss → Herbaceous plants → Shrub → Forest

Pioneer species (lichens) colonize bare rock, weather it, build soil, allowing larger plants to establish.
questions.knowledgeNote: Climax community = stable end stage. Hydrosere = succession in water.

questions.question: A grassland ecosystem has a gross primary productivity of 4800 kcal m^-2 yr^-1 and plant respiration of 1200 kcal m^-2 yr^-1. (a) Calculate the net primary productivity. (b) If herbivore respiration is 400 kcal m^-2 yr^-1 and all the NPP is consumed by herbivores, how much energy is passed to the next trophic level as secondary production?
questions.solution:
**Given:** GPP = 4800 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹; respiration of plants (R) = 1200 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹; respiration of herbivores (R₂) = 400 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.

**Step 1 — Net primary productivity (NPP)**

NPP is the amount of food energy actually stored as plant biomass after the plants have used some of the GPP for their own respiration.

$$\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R = 4800 - 1200 = 3600\ \text{kcal m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$$

**Step 2 — Secondary production of herbivores**

The energy that herbivores store as their own body tissue (secondary production) is what they ingest minus what they burn in respiration.

$$\text{Secondary production} = \text{NPP} - R_2 = 3600 - 400 = 3200\ \text{kcal m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$$

$$\text{Energy passed to carnivores} = 3200\ \text{kcal m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$$

**Interpretations:**
- The plants of this grassland keep 3600 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ (75% of GPP) as net biomass; **primary productivity = NPP**, not GPP.
- The value is high here only because *all* the NPP was assumed to be eaten. In a natural ecosystem only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next (**Lindeman's ten percent rule**), because most is lost as respiration, heat, excretion and to decomposers.
questions.knowledgeNote: NPP equals GPP minus plant respiration, and by the ten percent rule only about a tenth of energy passes to the next trophic level.

questions.question: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection with an example.
questions.solution:
**Darwin's theory (1859):** Organisms produce more offspring than can survive. Individuals with favorable variations survive and reproduce (natural selection). Over generations, favorable traits become common.

**Postulates:**
1. Overproduction — more offspring produced
2. Variation — individuals differ
3. Struggle for existence — limited resources
4. Survival of the fittest — better adapted survive
5. Heredity — favorable traits passed on

**Example:** Industrial melanism in moths — dark moths survived better in soot-covered trees during Industrial Revolution.
questions.knowledgeNote: Darwin called it 'descent with modification.' Modern synthesis combines Darwin with genetics.

questions.question: What are the evidences of evolution? Explain with one example each from morphological and paleontological studies.
questions.solution:
**Morphological evidence:** Homologous structures — same basic plan, different functions. Example: Forelimbs of humans, whales, bats (all have same bone pattern but different uses).

**Paleontological evidence:** Fossils in rock strata show progression from simple to complex. Example: Archaeopteryx (transitional fossil between reptiles and birds).
questions.knowledgeNote: Homologous = common ancestry; analogous = convergent evolution (similar function, different origin).

questions.question: Describe the Miller-Urey experiment on the origin of life, stating the chemicals used and the products obtained, and comment on its significance.
questions.solution:
In 1953 **Stanley Miller**, working under **Stanley L. Miller and Harold Urey** at the University of Chicago, attempted to demonstrate the chemical evolution of life on the early Earth.

**Apparatus:**
- A closed, **sterile glass flask** containing water, with the upper part filled with a mixture of gases.
- Two **tungsten electrodes** were placed in the flask and an **electric spark (electric discharge)** was passed repeatedly between them, simulating lightning and giving energy.
- The water below was **boiled** so that steam rose; the steam passed through a **water-cooled condenser**, condensed, and the droplets fell back into the boiling chamber — a continuous **circulation cycle**.

**Chemicals used (the assumed early-Earth atmosphere):** a **reducing atmosphere** with no free oxygen — methane (CH₄), ammonia (NH₃), hydrogen (H₂) and water vapour (H₂O).

**Procedure:** The apparatus was sealed and **boiled for one week** while electric sparks were passed continuously.

**Products obtained:** After a week, organic compounds appeared in the flask. **Paper chromatography and ion-exchange chromatography** revealed **amino acids** such as glycine, alanine and aspartic acid; later analysis of the same tar found more than 20 amino acids, together with sugars, fatty acids and adenine. The dark brown polymer formed was named a **coacervate** precursor material.

**Significance:**
1. It was the **first strong experimental evidence** that **complex organic molecules can be built up abiotically** from simple inorganic gases in a reducing atmosphere — it supported the **Oparin–Haldane primordial soup (chemical evolution) hypothesis**.
2. It indicates that the raw materials of life (amino acids, sugars) could form without living organisms, and life arose later from such organic molecules.

**Limitation:** Modern geology suggests the early atmosphere was only **weakly reducing** and was dominated by N₂, CO₂ and H₂O, so Miller's strongly reducing mixture does not fully represent the real early Earth.
questions.knowledgeNote: Miller-Urey showed that amino acids form from methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour when sparks pass through a reducing atmosphere.

questions.question: Differentiate between homologous and analogous organs with one example of each, and state which organ is better evidence of evolution and why.
questions.solution:
**Homologous organs**
- Similar in **structure and origin**, but perform **different functions**.
- Inherited from a **common ancestor**; they are evidence of **divergent evolution**.
- Example: the **forelimb of man, whale, bat and cheetah** all contain the same basic plan — humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges — but function as hand, flipper, wing and running leg respectively.

**Analogous organs**
- Different in **structure and origin**, but perform the **same function**.
- Evolved independently in unrelated groups under similar environmental pressure; they are evidence of **convergent evolution**.
- Example: the **wings of a butterfly and of a bird** perform the same function (flight) but butterfly wings are folded cuticle with veins while bird wings are modified forelimbs with feathers. Similarly, the phylloclade of *Opuntia* and the phyllode of *Acacia* are analogous.

| Basis | Homologous | Analogous |
|---|---|---|
| Structure and origin | Same structure, same origin | Different structure, different origin |
| Function | Different functions | Same function |
| Evolution | Divergent | Convergent |
| Example | Human arm and whale flipper | Butterfly wing and bird wing |

**Which is better evidence and why?**
**Homologous organs** are stronger evidence of evolution, because similarity in the same basic structural plan can only be explained by **descent with modification from a common ancestor**; it is a direct record of evolutionary history. Analogous similarity results only from similar function in similar habitats and so does not indicate common ancestry.
questions.knowledgeNote: Homologous organs share structure and origin but differ in function; analogous organs share function but differ in structure and origin.

questions.question: Write the diagnostic features of the phylum Arthropoda. Give one example.
questions.solution:
**Phylum Arthropoda** (largest animal phylum):
1. Jointed appendages
2. Chitinous exoskeleton
3. Segmental body (head, thorax, abdomen)
4. Open circulatory system
5. Tracheal/gill respiration
6. Well-developed sense organs

Example: Periplaneta (cockroach), Palaemon (prawn), Limulus (king crab)
questions.knowledgeNote: Arthropoda includes insects (75% of known species), arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods.

questions.question: Describe the characteristic features of phylum Arthropoda and its main classes with one example of each.
questions.solution:
**Phylum Arthropoda** (Gr. *arthron* = joint, *podos* = foot) is the **largest phylum of the animal kingdom**, with over one million species. The name means **jointed foot**.

**Characteristic features:**
1. **Body is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and segmented** — head, thorax and abdomen in insects.
2. **Chitinous exoskeleton** — an external skeleton of chitin and protein; it does not grow, so it is cast off periodically. This moulting is called **ecdysis**.
3. **Jointed appendages** for locomotion — the basis of the name.
4. Body cavity is a reduced coelom plus a large **haemocoel**; **open circulatory system** with haemolymph; **tetragastric** gut.
5. **Respiration** by gills (crustaceans), **tracheal tubes** (insects, myriapods), **book lungs** (arachnids) or body surface.
6. **Excretion** by **green (coxal) glands** or **Malpighian tubules**; usually dioecious with direct or indirect (larval) development.

**Main classes:**
- **Insecta** — body divided into head, thorax and abdomen; **six jointed legs**, two antennae, three pairs of wings in many forms. Examples: housefly (*Musca domestica*), grasshopper, butterfly, honeybee, ant.
- **Arachnida** — body divided into cephalothorax and abdomen; **eight legs (four pairs)**, no antennae. Examples: spider (*Argiope*), scorpion, tick, mite.
- **Crustacea** — body divided into cephalothorax and abdomen; **ten legs**, gills for respiration, often calcified exoskeleton. Examples: lobster, prawn, crab, **crayfish (Nepal)**.
- **Diplopoda (millipede)** — many body segments, **two pairs of legs per segment**, herbivorous. Example: *Glomeris*.
- **Chilopoda (centipede)** — many segments, **one pair of legs per segment**, venomous claws, carnivorous. Example: *Scolopendra*.

**Importance:** Arthropods are **decomposers** and **pollinators**, are a food source for fisheries, and include serious agricultural pests such as the locust (*Locusta migratoria*) and the red cotton bug.
questions.knowledgeNote: Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum; insects have six legs, arachnids eight and crustaceans ten, all with a chitinous exoskeleton.

questions.question: Describe the respiratory system of frog.
questions.solution:
**Frog respiration is multiple:**

1. **Cutaneous** (skin) — moist skin allows gas exchange underwater; important in hibernation.
2. ** Buccal** (mouth cavity) — rhythmic pumping moves air.
3. **Pulmonary** (lungs) — simple sacs with internal folds; primary mode on land.

**Mechanism:** Frog breathes by positive pressure ventilation — fills mouth with air, closes nostrils, pushes air into lungs via buccal pumping.
questions.knowledgeNote: Frog skin is permeable to water and gases. Tadpoles breathe via gills.

questions.question: Describe the general characteristics of the phylum Bryophyta. Give two economic importance.
questions.solution:
**Characteristics:**
- Small, non-vascular plants (no true roots, stems, leaves)
- Dominant gametophyte generation
- Require water for fertilization
- Thalloid or leafy body
- Examples: Marchantia, Funaria

**Economic importance:**
1. Peat moss (Sphagnum) — fuel, packing material
2. Used as ornamental plants; some used in traditional medicine
questions.knowledgeNote: Bryophytes are 'amphibians of plant kingdom' — need water for reproduction.

questions.question: Differentiate between dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous angiosperms with one example of each.
questions.solution:
Angiosperms are divided into **Dicotyledonae (dicots)** and **Monocotyledonae (monocots)**:

| Feature | Dicotyledonae (dicots) | Monocotyledonae (monocots) |
|---|---|---|
| **Cotyledons** | **Two** cotyledons in the seed | **One** cotyledon (the scutellum) |
| **Leaf venation** | **Reticulate (net-like)** | **Parallel** |
| **Root system** | **Tap root** bearing lateral roots; shows secondary growth | **Fibrous/adventitious** root system; no secondary growth |
| **Stem** | Vascular bundles arranged in a **ring**; has vascular cambium and shows secondary growth | Vascular bundles **scattered** in the ground tissue; no cambium |
| **Flower** | Parts in **fours or fives** — 5 sepals, 5 petals, 5 stamens, 2 carpels | Parts in **threes or multiples of three** — 5 sepals absent, usually 3+3 per whorl |
| **Stomata** | Present on **both** surfaces of the leaf | Present mostly on the **lower** surface only |
| **Pollen grains** | **Tricolpate** (three colpi) | **Monocolpate** (one colpus) |
| **Examples** | Potato (*Solanum tuberosum*), tomato, pea (*Pisum*), mustard (*Brassica*) | Onion (*Allium cepa*), maize (*Zea mays*), rice, wheat, sugarcane |

**Conclusion:** Dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate venation and a ring of vascular bundles, whereas monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation and scattered vascular bundles.
questions.knowledgeNote: Dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate venation and a tap root; monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation and fibrous roots.

questions.question: Differentiate between basic research and applied research with two examples of each.
questions.solution:
| Basis | Basic (pure) research | Applied research |
|---|---|---|
| Aim | To gain **knowledge** for its own sake | To solve a **practical problem** |
| Motivation | Curiosity, no immediate utility | Immediate usefulness for society |
| Outcome | Principles, concepts, theories, laws | New technology, products, processes |
| Examples | Watson and Crick's model of the DNA double helix; Mendel's laws of inheritance; the mechanism of photosynthesis | Norman Borlaug's development of high-yielding, disease-resistant wheat (Green Revolution); production of vaccines; use of *Penicillium* to make penicillin |

**Relation:** Every applied research rests on the knowledge gained by basic research. Development of a new vaccine or hybrid maize began with basic studies of the germ theory of disease and of the law of segregation, respectively.
questions.knowledgeNote: Basic research is research for knowledge; applied research uses that knowledge to solve real problems and is built upon it.

questions.question: Describe the steps of the biological method of investigation with a suitable example.
questions.solution:
The **biological method** is the systematic, logical procedure used to solve a biological problem. Its main steps are:

1. **Observation** — carefully and repeatedly noticing a natural event, e.g. noticing that boiled milk stays fresh longer than raw milk, or that a glass of water with a slice of mango develops a fuzzy growth after some days.
2. **Question / Problem** — converting the observation into a clear, testable question, e.g. *Does dust or living particles cause the spoilage?* (Louis Pasteur's problem).
3. **Hypothesis** — a tentative, testable explanation, e.g. *'Life arises spontaneously in decaying matter and the fuzzy growth is caused by dust-borne living organisms.'*
4. **Experimentation** — testing the hypothesis under controlled conditions with a control. Pasteur put broth in a straight-necked flask (boiled, sterile, open to air) and in a **swan-neck flask** (boiled, sterile, air entering through a bent tube); the straight neck admitted dust while the swan neck trapped dust particles.
5. **Observation and analysis of data** — recording and tabulating the results (which flask developed life, after how many days).
6. **Conclusion** — the hypothesis is accepted, modified or rejected. Conclusion: growth occurred only in the straight-necked flask, so life does **not** arise spontaneously; dust-borne micro-organisms cause spoilage.
7. **Formulation of theory and law** — a well-substantiated explanation becomes a **theory**, and a concise statement of an always-observed relationship becomes a **law** (e.g. the law of biogenesis).

The biological method is essentially the **scientific method** applied to living phenomena.
questions.knowledgeNote: The biological method runs observation to question, hypothesis, experiment, analysis and conclusion; Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask refuted spontaneous generation.

questions.question: Describe any five branches of biology with one example of the kind of problem studied in each.
questions.solution:
Biology is a vast science and is divided into many branches:

1. **Botany** — the study of plants. Example: studying the floral anatomy and placentation of the tomato plant (*Solanum lycopersicum*).
2. **Zoology** — the study of animals. Example: classifying the wild animals of the Terai grasslands such as the one-horned rhinoceros (*Rhinoceros unicornis*).
3. **Microbiology** — the study of microscopic organisms. Example: culturing *Escherichia coli* on nutrient agar to study bacterial growth.
4. **Genetics** — the study of heredity and variation. Example: Mendel's cross experiments on garden pea (*Pisum sativum*).
5. **Ecology** — the study of the interrelationship of organisms with their environment. Example: studying the food relationships in a grassland of the Kathmandu Valley.
6. **Physiology** — the study of the functions of the body and its organs. Example: studying how the nephron of the kidney filters blood and forms urine.
7. **Cytology** — the study of the cell. Example: observing mitosis in the root tip of onion (*Allium cepa*).
8. **Biotechnology** — the practical application of biology and molecular biology. Example: production of human insulin by recombinant DNA technology, or PCR amplification of DNA.
questions.knowledgeNote: Botany studies plants, zoology animals, microbiology micro-organisms, genetics heredity and ecology organism–environment relationships.

questions.question: Which one of the following is the first step of the biological method of investigation? (a) Formulating a hypothesis (b) Making an observation (c) Designing an experiment (d) Drawing a conclusion
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (b) Making an observation**

**Reasoning:**
- The biological method **begins with a careful, objective observation** of a natural event. This observation creates curiosity and raises a problem, out of which a proper question is framed. ✔
- A **hypothesis** (a) comes only *after* the observation and the question — a hypothesis proposed without any observation is merely an imagination, not science. ✘
- An **experiment** (c) is designed to *test* the hypothesis, so it is a later step. ✘
- A **conclusion** (d) is drawn only after all observations and experiments are over. ✘

Hence, the correct answer is **(b) Making an observation**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Observation is the first and indispensable step of the biological method; a hypothesis without observation is unfounded.

questions.question: Describe the structure and mode of reproduction of a bacteriophage (T2 phage) and state two uses of bacteriophages.
questions.solution:
A **bacteriophage** is a virus that attacks bacteria. Its structure was first revealed by **Bradley and Kay (1951)** with the electron microscope, using **T2 phage of *Escherichia coli***.

**Structure of T2 bacteriophage:**
1. **Icosahedral head (capsid)** — made of protein subunits called **capsomeres**.
2. **Nucleic core** inside the head — a molecule of **double-stranded DNA** (the genetic material).
3. **Neck/collar (head-piece)** joining head and tail.
4. **Tail sheath** — a helical protein sheath.
5. **Hollow tail tube (tail core)** through which the DNA is injected.
6. **Base plate or end plate** carrying **tail fibres** (with receptor-binding tips) and **pins/spikes**, which fix the phage onto the bacterial cell.
The overall shape is like a tadpole or a hypodermic syringe.

**Mode of reproduction — lytic cycle:**
1. **Attachment (adsorption)** — tail fibres recognise and bind to specific receptor sites on the living *E. coli* cell wall.
2. **Penetration** — the sheath contracts, the tail pierces the wall and the phage DNA is injected into the cytoplasm; the empty protein coat stays outside.
3. **Synthesis (biosynthesis)** — the bacterial enzymes are hijacked to make many copies of phage DNA and of phage proteins.
4. **Assembly (maturation)** — 100 or more complete phage particles are assembled inside the host.
5. **Lysis and release** — the phage releases an enzyme (lysozyme) that digests the bacterial cell wall, the cell bursts and releases about 100–200 new bacteriophages.

*In some phages the DNA instead integrates into the bacterial chromosome as a **prophage** and is replicated with the host (**lysogenic cycle**) until it is induced into the lytic cycle.*

**Two uses of bacteriophages:**
1. **Phage therapy / biological control** — specific phages are used to kill disease-causing bacteria in humans and animals without harming beneficial bacteria, and to control plant and animal pathogens.
2. **Genetic engineering and research** — phages act as **cloning vectors** to carry foreign DNA into bacteria, and the **Hershey–Chase experiment (1952)** with ³²P-labelled DNA and ³⁵S-labelled protein proved that **DNA, not protein, is the genetic material** of phages.
questions.knowledgeNote: T2 phage of E. coli has a DNA-filled icosahedral head, tail sheath and tail fibres; in the lytic cycle it reproduces and bursts the host cell.

questions.question: Describe the major vegetation zones of Nepal with their approximate altitudinal ranges and two typical species of each.
questions.solution:
The vegetation of Nepal changes with **altitude**, because temperature falls by about **6.5 °C for every 1000 m** of rise. This gives the following altitudinal belts:

| Zone | Approx. altitude | Vegetation | Two typical species |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tropical (Terai, Bhabar) | up to ~1000 m | Tropical deciduous / sal forest | *Shorea robusta* (sal), *Acacia nilotica* (babar) |
| Subtropical | ~1000–2000 m | Mixed evergreen and deciduous forest | *Schima* castanopsis, *Albizia* spp. |
| Temperate | ~2000–3000 m | Broad-leaved deciduous forest, rhododendron | *Quercus* (oak), *Acer* (maple) |
| Subalpine | ~3000–3500 m | Temperate coniferous forest | *Cedrus deodara* (deodar), *Abies spectabilis* (fir) |
| Alpine | ~3500–5000 m | Alpine shrub, rhododendron scrub and meadow | *Juniperus squamata*, *Nardostachys jatamansi* |
| Nival | above ~5000 m | Bare rock, snow, lichens and mosses only | *Sagarmatha* (Mt. Everest), *Annapurna* |

**Notes:**
- The **treeline** in the Himalaya lies near 4000 m, above which no proper trees grow.
- About 12% of Nepal lies above 3000 m and only about 5% lies above the treeline, so the nival and alpine zones are very small.
- Vegetation also changes **horizontally** — tropical forest dominates the southern Terai, while coniferous and alpine vegetation dominate the northern Himalaya.
questions.knowledgeNote: Nepal has six altitudinal vegetation belts from tropical to nival, with temperature falling roughly 6.5 °C per 1000 m rise.

questions.question: Which one of the following vegetation types occurs at the highest altitude in Nepal? (a) Tropical deciduous forest (b) Broad-leaved temperate forest (c) Temperate coniferous forest (d) Alpine scrub and meadow (tundra)
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (d) Alpine scrub and meadow (tundra)**

**Reasoning:**
- Temperature decreases by about **6.5 °C for every 1000 m** of rise in altitude, so the higher the zone the colder and more severe the climate. ✔
- The **treeline** in the Nepal Himalaya lies near **4000 m**. Above it only dwarf, cushion-form, creeping shrubs and hardy grasses survive — e.g. *Nardostachys jatamansi*, *Juniperus squamata* and alpine *Rhododendron*. This is the **alpine scrub and meadow**. ✔
- The **temperate coniferous forest** (c) occurs lower, at about **3000–3500 m**, and requires 1500–3000 mm of precipitation. ✘
- The **broad-leaved temperate forest** (b) (2000–3000 m) and the **tropical deciduous forest** (a) (below 1000 m) are still lower. ✘
- Above about 5200 m only bare rock, snow, lichens and mosses remain — the **nival** zone — which is below the alpine meadow in terms of vegetation development but above it in altitude. However, among the *vegetation types* listed, the alpine scrub and meadow is the highest. ✔

Hence the correct answer is **(d)**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Above the treeline near 4000 m in Nepal only alpine scrub and meadow, lichens and mosses survive — the nival zone is bare rock and snow.

questions.question: Describe the vegetation found in the Terai and Bhabar zones of Nepal, mentioning four important species.
questions.solution:
**Location:** The **Terai** is the southern lowland belt of Nepal, lying roughly between 200 m and 600 m altitude, running below the Siwalik hills. It is hot, humid and receives 150–200 cm or more of rain, most of it in the monsoon. The **Bhabar** zone lies between about 200 m and 400 m and is a belt of porous alluvium where many streams disappear underground.

**Vegetation of the Bhabar:** Open scrub and deciduous forest on the dry, porous alluvium — *Dalbergia sissoo* (shisham), bamboo (*Dendrocalamus*), *Acacia nilotica*, and the invasive shrub *Lantana camara*.

**Vegetation of the Terai:** Tall, dense **mixed deciduous forest** and **sal forest**, with some evergreen patches along the rivers (Karnali, Narayani, Kosi).

**Four important species:**
1. *Shorea robusta* (**sal**) — dominant canopy tree; timber tree.
2. *Dalbergia sissoo* (**shisham**) — fast-growing timber tree.
3. *Acacia nilotica* (**babar**) — thorny nitrogen-fixing tree of the doon.
4. *Bauhinia variegata* (**narikhaj**) — showy-flowered tree; a typical Terai tree.

Other trees include *Salmalia malabarica* (simal/silk cotton), *Ficus glomerata* (gular) and *Terminalia arjuna* (arjun).

**Importance:** The Terai vegetation shelters the one-horned rhinoceros, Bengal tiger, elephant and swamp deer, and provides fuel, timber, timber products and grazing land for the densely populated southern plain.
questions.knowledgeNote: The Terai carries tall mixed deciduous and sal forest; shisham, babar, narikhaj and sal are its signature trees.

questions.question: Differentiate between the temperate coniferous forest and the broad-leaved temperate forest of Nepal.
questions.solution:
**1. Temperate coniferous forest** (about 3000–3500 m)
- Trees are **conifers**, bearing **cones (strobili)** — *Abies spectabilis* (fir), *Cedrus deodara* (deodar), *Pinus wallichiana* (chir pine), *Cupressus*.
- Leaves are **needle-shaped** with a **thick cuticle and waxy coating** and **sunken stomata**, so transpiration is minimum.
- Trees are **evergreen**; branches are **flexible and conical**, allowing heavy snow to slide off.
- Need moderately high precipitation (1500–3000 mm) and cold, dry winters.

**2. Broad-leaved temperate forest** (about 2000–3000 m)
- Trees bear **broad, flat leaves** — oaks (*Quercus*), *Acer*, *Castanopsis*, *Rhododendron*.
- Trees are **deciduous** and **shed their leaves in autumn** before the onset of cold and snow.
- The shed leaf litter protects the soil from frost and adds humus.
- A mixed conifer–broadleaf belt occurs where the two zones meet.

**Common features of both:**
Both are temperate, occur below the alpine zone, provide grazing land in summer, and are important for soil and water conservation.
questions.knowledgeNote: Conifers keep needle leaves with sunken stomata and shed snow-laden branches; temperate broad-leaved trees are deciduous and shed leaves in autumn.

questions.question: Describe the chemical changes involved in black-and-white photography, from exposure of the photographic plate to fixing of the print. Give balanced equations.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Preparation of the plate.** A glass or celluloid plate is coated with a gelatin film containing finely divided **silver bromide**, which is pale yellow and light-sensitive.

**Step 2 — Exposure.** Light energy reduces the silver ions to metallic silver, giving a latent image:

$$2\text{AgBr} \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2\text{Ag} + \text{Br}_2$$

**Step 3 — Developing.** The latent image is intensified by an organic reducing agent such as hydroquinone or potassium thiosulphate solution, converting more exposed AgBr into black metallic silver.

**Step 4 — Stopping and fixing.** The film is fixed in a solution of sodium thiosulphate, which dissolves the unexposed silver bromide so that further light no longer affects it. A wash in hypo solution is followed by washing in running water:

$$\text{AgBr} + 2\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{Na}_3[\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2] + \text{NaBr}$$

The areas where silver was deposited print as black; the fixed areas print as the white of the paper.
questions.knowledgeNote: Light reduces AgBr to silver metal; sodium thiosulphate fixes the print by dissolving unexposed AgBr as a soluble complex.

questions.question: Explain why an alloy is usually harder and stronger than the pure metal. Give the composition of brass and explain why it is preferred to pure gold for making ornaments and musical instruments.
questions.solution:
**Why alloys are harder.**

1. The atoms of the second metal are larger than those of the host metal, so in the alloy they cannot fit neatly into the regular lattice of the pure metal. The lattice becomes distorted and the layers are prevented from sliding over one another.
2. The solute atoms obstruct the movement of dislocation, so a much greater force is needed for plastic deformation — the alloy becomes harder and stronger but less ductile.
3. Alloying also raises the melting point and increases corrosion resistance.

**Brass** is an alloy of **copper (70–90%) and zinc (10–30%)**.

**Why preferred over pure gold.** Pure gold is extremely soft (very malleable) and scratches easily, and it is very costly. Brass is hard, durable, corrosion-resistant, has a golden shine, and is far cheaper. Hence brass is used for ornaments, buttons, taps and for bells, trumpets and other instruments where hardness and resonance matter.

**Stainless steel**, another common alloy, is iron with about 11% chromium and is used for kitchen utensils because chromium forms a protective oxide layer that resists rusting.
questions.knowledgeNote: Alloying distorts the crystal lattice and blocks dislocation movement, increasing hardness, strength and corrosion resistance.

questions.question: Describe the preparation and setting of plaster of Paris. Give balanced equations and state why it cannot be used as a permanent building material.
questions.solution:
**Preparation.** Gypsum is heated in a kiln at about 373 K so that three-fourths of its water of crystallisation is lost:

$$2(\text{CaSO}_4\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O}) \xrightarrow{373 \ \text{K}} (\text{CaSO}_4)_2\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\uparrow$$

The product is **plaster of Paris** (hemihydrate, $(CaSO_4)_2\cdot H_2O$), a white powder.

**Setting.** When mixed with water it absorbs the water again and forms a hard interlocking mass of gypsum:

$$(\text{CaSO}_4)_2\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2(\text{CaSO}_4\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O})$$

The interlocking crystals expand slightly and bond to the wall.

**Why it is not a permanent material.** The hardened mass is **gypsum** $(CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O)$, not anhydrous calcium sulphate. In the presence of water it dissolves again to form hemihydrate, so the plaster is destroyed by rain or by water leakage. It is therefore used only for interior work, ceiling and false roofs, decorative work, casts and surgical plaster.

**Related reaction.** Gypsum is manufactured from limestone and sulphuric acid:
$$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Plaster of Paris, (CaSO₄)₂·H₂O, sets by absorbing water to form gypsum, so it dissolves again in water and is not permanent.

questions.question: Give the reaction of benzene with (a) a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids, (b) fuming sulphuric acid, and (c) chlorine in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride. State the conditions for each.
questions.solution:
**(a) Nitration — at about 323 K (50 °C), concentrated HNO₃ with concentrated H₂SO₄ as catalyst:**

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{HNO}_3 \xrightarrow[50^\circ\text{C}]{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Nitrobenzene is formed (an electrophilic substitution).

**(b) Sulphonation — with fuming (oleum) sulphuric acid at 100 °C:**

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \xrightarrow{100^\circ\text{C},\ \text{fuming}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Benzenesulphonic acid is formed; the reverse reaction occurs on dilution with water.

**(c) Halogenation — chlorine passed in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ catalyst:**

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{anh. AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$

Chlorobenzene is produced. The halogen must be dry, otherwise water hydrolyses the AlCl₃ catalyst and the reaction stops.
questions.knowledgeNote: Nitration needs conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ at 323 K, sulphonation needs fuming H₂SO₄, and chlorination needs anhydrous AlCl₃.

questions.question: What is resonance? Explain resonance in benzene by writing its contributing structures and state any two consequences of resonance in benzene.
questions.solution:
**Resonance** is the phenomenon in which a single molecule cannot be represented by one conventional structure but by two or more rapidly interchanging structures called **resonance (canonical) structures**. Only the hybrid of these is a real structure, and the true molecule is more stable than any single canonical form.

**In benzene.** Carbon 2 to 6 each possess one electron in an unhybridised p orbital. Overlap of these six parallel p orbitals delocalises the six electrons over the whole ring. The two Kekulé structures (double bonds at 1–2, 3–4, 5–6 and at 2–3, 4–5, 6–1) are the principal contributing structures:

Structure I: (1=2, 3=4, 5=6)  Structure II: (2=3, 4=5, 6=1)

**Consequences.**

1. **All six C–C bonds are identical.** Each bond length is 139 pm, exactly intermediate between a single bond (154 pm) and a double bond (134 pm). Kekulé's model predicted two different bond lengths and is therefore wrong.
2. **Greater stability than expected.** The resonance energy (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹) makes benzene much less reactive than cyclohexatriene; the double bonds behave as a delocalised π cloud rather than as three isolated bonds.
3. **No free rotation** about any C–C bond, and the molecule is completely planar and regular hexagonal.
questions.knowledgeNote: Benzene's six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, so all C–C bonds are equal at 139 pm.

questions.question: Explain why benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than electrophilic addition. Compare the directing effect of a –CH₃ group and a –NO₂ group in electrophilic aromatic substitution.
questions.solution:
**Why substitution, not addition.** Benzene has a large resonance energy (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹) and a delocalised π cloud of electron density above and below the ring. Attack by an electrophile temporarily disturbs and destroys this aromatic sextet, whereas substitution only replaces one H atom and the ring is restored as an aromatic ion. Addition therefore costs about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ and is energetically unfavourable, so substitution dominates.

**–CH₃ group (ortho/para directing).** Methyl has a $+I$ effect and hyperconjugation, so it raises the electron density of the ring. The electrophile is attracted to the electron-rich ring and attacks at ortho or para positions, where the intermediate cation is additionally stabilised by hyperconjugation from the methyl group. Example: nitration of toluene gives mainly o- and p-nitrotoluene.

**–NO₂ group (meta directing).** Nitro has a strong $-I$ effect and also $-M$ effect, withdrawing electron density and deactivating the ring. Attack at ortho or para puts a positive charge adjacent to the already positive nitrogen, which is very unstable, so attack occurs mainly at the meta position. Example: nitration of nitrobenzene gives mainly m-dinitrobenzene (about 93%).
questions.knowledgeNote: Aromatic substitution preserves the resonance-stabilised ring; –CH₃ activates and directs ortho/para, while –NO₂ deactivates and directs meta.

questions.question: Explain Aufbau's principle with an example.
questions.solution:
**Aufbau's principle:** Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy: 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p...

Example: Calcium (Z=20): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² — electrons fill 4s before 3d because 4s has lower energy.
questions.knowledgeNote: Use the (n+l) rule: lower (n+l) means lower energy. If equal, lower n fills first.

questions.question: The quantum numbers of an electron are given below. (a) n = 3, l = 1, mₗ = +1, mₛ = +1/2 (b) n = 3, l = 1, mₗ = +2, mₛ = −1/2 (c) n = 3, l = 1, mₗ = −1, mₛ = −1/2 (d) n = 3, l = 0, mₗ = 0, mₛ = +1/2. Which set of quantum numbers is not possible?
questions.solution:
The allowed rules are:

1. $l$ may have $(n-1)$ values, i.e. for $n = 3$, $l = 0, 1, 2$.
2. $m_l$ may take $(2l+1)$ values from $-l$ to $+l$.
3. $m_s$ is only $+1/2$ or $-1/2$.

Checking each set:

- **(a)** $l = 1$, $m_l = +1$ is allowed; $m_s = +1/2$ allowed. Possible.
- **(b)** $l = 1$, so $m_l$ can only be $-1, 0$ or $+1$. The value $m_l = +2$ is **not allowed**. Not possible.
- **(c)** $l = 1$, $m_l = -1$ and $m_s = -1/2$ are allowed. Possible (3p orbital).
- **(d)** $l = 0$ corresponds to the 3s subshell, $m_l = 0$ and either spin. Possible.

**Answer: (b)**
questions.knowledgeNote: For l = 1 the magnetic quantum number can take only the values −1, 0 or +1.

questions.question: Using $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \,/\, n^2$ J, calculate the energy of the electron in the second orbit of a hydrogen atom and the wavelength of the photon emitted when the electron falls from the third to the second orbit. Express the wavelength in nm.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Energy in the second orbit**

$$E_2 = \frac{-2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{2^2} = -5.45 \times 10^{-19} \ \text{J}$$

**Step 2 — Energy released in the transition**

$$\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right)$$

$$\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \frac{5}{36} = 3.03 \times 10^{-19} \ \text{J}$$

**Step 3 — Wavelength of the emitted photon**

$$\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{3.03 \times 10^{-19}}$$

$$\lambda = \frac{1.988 \times 10^{-25}}{3.03 \times 10^{-19}} = 6.56 \times 10^{-7} \ \text{m} = \textbf{656 nm}$$

The negative sign of $E_2$ shows that the electron is bound; energy must be supplied to remove it.
questions.knowledgeNote: This transition gives the red H-alpha line of the Balmer series, of wavelength about 656 nm.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC names of: (a) CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (b) CH₃CHO (c) HOCH₂CH₂OH (d) CH₃CH(CH₃)COOH.
questions.solution:
**(a) CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH.** The longest chain with the carboxyl carbon has 4 carbons; the acid suffix is '-oic acid'.

**Butanoic acid**

**(b) CH₃CHO.** The longest chain has 2 carbons and the aldehyde carbon is always C1; the suffix is '-al'.

**Ethanal**

**(c) HOCH₂CH₂OH.** The longest chain has 2 carbons and carries two hydroxyl groups, so the parent is ethane with the ending '-diol'.

**Ethane-1,2-diol**

**(d) CH₃CH(CH₃)COOH.** The longest chain with the –COOH carbon has 3 carbons, and a methyl group is on C2.

**2-Methylpropanoic acid**

Remember the priority order of characteristic groups: carboxylic acid > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine. The characteristic group is always included in the parent chain and must receive the lowest locant.
questions.knowledgeNote: Carboxylic acids use the '-oic acid' ending with the COOH carbon numbered 1; alcohols use '-ol'.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name of the compound CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂OH.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Choose the parent chain.** The longest continuous chain containing the –OH group has six carbon atoms, so the parent is **hexane**. The –OH carbon must be numbered as C1.

$$\text{C1 (CH}_2\text{OH)} - \text{C2 [CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_3)]} - \text{C3 (CH}_2\text{) - C4 (CH}_2\text{) - C5 [CH(CH}_3\text{)] - C6 (CH}_3\text{)}$$

**Step 2 — Number the chain.** Numbering from the –OH end gives the hydroxy group locant 1; numbering from the other end would give it locant 6, which is not permitted.

**Step 3 — Identify substituents.** An ethyl group on C2 and a methyl group on C5.

**Step 4 — Assemble the name,** listing substituents alphabetically (ethyl before methyl) and adding the position and form of the suffix:

$$\boxed{\text{2-ethyl-5-methylhexan-1-ol}}$$

A hyphen is placed before a single-letter or single-digit prefix, and the final 'e' of the '-ane' is dropped before the vowel of '-ol'.
questions.knowledgeNote: The longest chain containing the –OH group is the parent, and numbering must give the hydroxy group the lowest locant.

questions.question: Define a functional group and a homologous series. State any three characteristics of a homologous series, and write the general formula of the alkanol series with two examples.
questions.solution:
**Functional group.** An atom or group of atoms present in every member of a family of organic compounds that largely determines its chemical properties, e.g. –OH (alcohols), –COOH (carboxylic acids), –CHO (aldehydes).

**Homologous series.** A family of organic compounds that differ from one another by one or more –CH₂– units and have similar chemical properties but gradually varying physical properties, e.g. CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH.

**Three characteristics.**

1. All members contain the same functional group and behave chemically alike.
2. Consecutive members differ by a CH₂ unit, i.e. by 14 mass units.
3. They are represented by a general formula, and physical properties such as boiling point, melting point and density change gradually and regularly with increasing molecular mass.
4. Physical properties change gradually but chemical properties remain the same.

**Alkanols.** Functional group –OH joined to a saturated carbon. General formula:

$$\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$$

Members are methanol $CH_3OH$ (b.p. 64.7 °C), ethanol $C_2H_5OH$ (78 °C), propan-1-ol $C_3H_7OH$ (97 °C). The boiling points rise regularly by about 20–25 °C per CH₂ unit.
questions.knowledgeNote: A homologous series shares one functional group, has a general formula, and consecutive members differ by a CH₂ unit.

questions.question: Give the formula of chlorophyll and explain the role of magnesium in plants. What happens if there is a deficiency of magnesium in the soil?
questions.solution:
**Formula.** Chlorophyll has the molecular formula $C_{55}H_{72}MgN_4O_5$; chlorophyll a is $C_{55}H_{72}MgN_4O_5$ and chlorophyll b is $C_{55}H_{70}MgN_4O_6$.

**Structure and the role of Mg.** The chlorophyll molecule consists of a porphyrin ring containing four nitrogen atoms. At the centre of this ring sits a single $Mg^{2+}$ ion, which is held by coordinate bonds to the four pyrrole nitrogens of the ring. This $Mg^{2+}$ ion is essential for the chlorophyll molecule to absorb light, and through it chlorophyll carries out **photosynthesis**, converting solar energy into chemical energy in the synthesis of carbohydrates.

**Deficiency.** Magnesium is a **mobile** nutrient. When it is deficient in the soil, it is withdrawn from the older leaves and translocated to the young growing leaves. Consequently the older leaves lose their green colour and become pale yellow — this yellowing is called **chlorosis** — and the plant's growth and photosynthetic output fall, ultimately causing **stunted growth** and early leaf fall. Adding magnesium sulphate or dolomite to the soil restores the green colour.
questions.knowledgeNote: Chlorophyll C₅₅H₇₂MgN₄O₅ has a central Mg²⁺ ion; its deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves.

questions.question: Which of the following trace elements is essential for the formation of haemoglobin in the human body? (a) zinc (b) copper (c) iron (d) iodine
questions.solution:
Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein; each of its four haem groups has an $Fe^{2+}$ ion at the centre of a porphyrin ring, and this iron reversibly binds oxygen. Iron is therefore the essential trace element for haemoglobin formation.

Other micro-nutrients have different roles: **zinc** is needed for enzyme activity and growth, **copper** for iron utilisation and connective tissue, and **iodine** for the hormone thyroxine.

**Answer: (c) iron**

A deficiency of iron lowers the haemoglobin content of the blood, producing anaemia, for which iron-rich foods or ferrous sulphate tablets are prescribed.
questions.knowledgeNote: Iron is the central constituent of the haem group of haemoglobin; its deficiency causes anaemia.

questions.question: Explain the biological role of haemoglobin in blood. What is carboxy haemoglobin, and why is carbon monoxide poisoning fatal?
questions.solution:
**Haemoglobin** is the red iron-containing pigment of red blood corpuscles, with the formula $C_{2952}H_{4664}N_{812}O_{832}S_{8}Fe_4$. It is a conjugated protein in which each of the four $Fe^{2+}$ ions is held inside a porphyrin ring called **haem**, the combination being haemoglobin.

**Biological role.** It transports oxygen from the lungs to all the tissues of the body, and also carries some carbon dioxide back. Oxygen binds reversibly to $Fe^{2+}$:

$$\text{Hb} + 4\text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Hb(O}_2)_4$$

**Carboxy haemoglobin.** Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin to form a stable cherry-red compound:

$$\text{Hb} + 4\text{CO} \rightarrow \text{Hb(CO)}_4 \qquad (\text{carboxyhaemoglobin})$$

**Why it is fatal.** CO binds to the $Fe^{2+}$ of haemoglobin about **250 times more avidly** than oxygen does, and the complex formed is far more stable and is not readily dissociated. Even a small concentration of CO in air (about 0.1%) saturates the haemoglobin completely, so no oxygen can reach the tissues. This produces severe hypoxia of all the tissues and organs, leading to unconsciousness and death within a few minutes.
questions.knowledgeNote: Haemoglobin carries O₂ through Fe²⁺; CO binds about 250 times more strongly, forming carboxyhaemoglobin that cannot release oxygen.

questions.question: Using valence bond theory, explain the formation of sigma and pi bonds in ethene, C₂H₄. State the hybridisation of each carbon atom and the H–C–H bond angle.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Structure.**

Each carbon in C₂H₄ has 4 valence electrons; one is used in a double bond and three in single bonds, so each carbon is bonded to three other atoms. Steric number = 3, hence each carbon is **sp² hybridised**.

**Step 2 — Sigma bonds.**

Three sp² hybrids on each carbon lie in one plane at $120^\circ$ to each other. Two of them overlap with the 1s orbitals of H atoms (C–H σ bonds) and the third overlaps head-on with an sp² hybrid of the other carbon.

$$\text{Total } \sigma \text{ bonds} = 4(\text{C–H}) + 1(\text{C–C}) = 5 \ \sigma \text{ bonds}$$

**Step 3 — Pi bond.**

Each carbon retains one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the plane. These two orbitals overlap sideways (laterally) to form one π bond.

$$\text{Total } \pi \text{ bonds} = 1$$

Hence the C=C double bond = 1 σ + 1 π. All six atoms are coplanar and $\angle \text{H–C–H} = 120^\circ$. Rotation about the C=C bond is restricted because it would break the π bond.
questions.knowledgeNote: In ethene each sp² carbon forms three σ bonds, and one unhybridised 2p orbital forms the single π bond.

questions.question: Predict the shape, hybridisation and bond angle of the following molecules using VSEPR theory: (a) PCl₅ (b) SF₆ (c) BeCl₂ (d) H₂S.
questions.solution:
**(a) PCl₅** — P has 5 valence electrons, all used in bonding; no lone pair. Steric number = 5 → **sp³d**, shape **trigonal bipyramidal**. Three equatorial bonds at $120^\circ$, axial–equatorial at $90^\circ$, axial–axial at $180^\circ$.

**(b) SF₆** — S has 6 valence electrons, all used in bonding; no lone pair. Steric number = 6 → **sp³d²**, shape **octahedral**. All adjacent bonds at $90^\circ$ and opposite pairs at $180^\circ$.

**(c) BeCl₂** — Be has only 2 valence electrons and forms 2 bonds with no lone pair. Steric number = 2 → **sp**, shape **linear**, angle $180^\circ$.

**(d) H₂S** — S has 6 valence electrons; 2 are used in bonding and 2 lone pairs remain. Steric number = 4 → approximately **sp³**, shape **bent (angular/V-shaped)**. The two lone pairs squeeze the bonds together so the angle is slightly less than the tetrahedral value, about **$92^\circ$** (compare $104.5^\circ$ in water, where O is more electronegative and the lone pairs are held closer to the nucleus).
questions.knowledgeNote: Five and six electron domains give trigonal bipyramidal (sp³d) and octahedral (sp³d²) shapes respectively.

questions.question: Using VSEPR theory, explain the shape of the ammonia molecule, its hybridisation and its bond angle. Why is its bond angle less than that of methane?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Electron domains.**

In NH₃, nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. Three are used in making three N–H σ bonds and one lone pair remains. So the steric number = 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 4.

**Step 2 — Hybridisation and shape.**

Four electron domains require sp³ hybridisation, giving a tetrahedral arrangement of the four hybrids. Only three are bonded, so the molecular shape is **trigonal pyramidal**.

**Step 3 — Bond angle.**

A pure tetrahedral angle is $109^\circ 28'$. The lone pair occupies more space than a bond pair (lone pair–bond pair repulsion > bond pair–bond pair repulsion) and pushes the three N–H bonds closer together.

$$\angle \text{H–N–H} = 107^\circ$$

In CH₄ there are four bond pairs and no lone pair, so no such compression occurs and the angle is the full tetrahedral **$109^\circ 28'$**.
questions.knowledgeNote: NH₃ is sp³ hybridised and trigonal pyramidal; its lone pair compresses the H–N–H angle to 107°.

questions.question: State Le Chatelier's principle. Predict the effect of increasing pressure on: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
questions.solution:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the change.

Increasing pressure favors the side with fewer moles of gas.
Reactants: 1+3 = 4 moles; Products: 2 moles.
Equilibrium shifts **towards NH₃ (right)** — Haber's process uses high pressure for this reason.
questions.knowledgeNote: If Δn = 0, pressure change has no effect on equilibrium position.

questions.question: For the reaction $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$, $K_c = 0.5$ at a certain temperature. If $[N_2] = 1.0$ M and $[H_2] = 0.5$ M at equilibrium, calculate the equilibrium concentration of ammonia.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Write the equilibrium constant expression**

The coefficient 3 on $H_2$ becomes a cube and the coefficient 2 on $NH_3$ becomes a square:

$$K_c = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3}$$

**Step 2 — Substitute the values**

$$0.5 = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{1.0 \times (0.5)^3}$$

$$[\text{NH}_3]^2 = 0.5 \times 1.0 \times 0.125 = 0.0625$$

**Step 3 — Take the square root**

$$[\text{NH}_3] = \sqrt{0.0625} = 0.25 \ \text{M}$$

Hence the equilibrium concentration of ammonia is **0.25 M**. Notice that the very small value of $K_c$ is consistent with ammonia being formed only slowly at that temperature.
questions.knowledgeNote: Stoichiometric coefficients become powers in the equilibrium constant: $K_c = [NH₃]^2/([N₂][H₂]^3)$.

questions.question: For the equilibrium $N_2O_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)$, $\Delta H = +57$ kJ mol⁻¹, state and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium of: (a) increasing the pressure, (b) lowering the temperature, (c) adding more $N_2O_4$ at constant volume.
questions.solution:
By Le Chatelier's principle, a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose the imposed change.

**(a) Increasing the pressure → equilibrium shifts to the right (towards $NO_2$).**

On the left there is 1 mole of gas and on the right 2 moles. Increased pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles, so it opposes the volume decrease by converting $N_2O_4$ into $NO_2$. Here the greater number of moles is the more stable side at high pressure, so the shift is to the right.

**(b) Lowering the temperature → equilibrium shifts to the left (towards $N_2O_4$).**

The forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$), so heat behaves as a product. Cooling removes heat, and the system compensates by favouring the exothermic reverse reaction. Hence $N_2O_4$ forms and the colour lightens.

**(c) Adding $N_2O_4$ at constant volume → equilibrium shifts to the right.**

The concentration of $N_2O_4$ increases, so the system consumes some of the added $N_2O_4$ to restore the original concentrations. $K_c$ itself is unchanged, since temperature has not changed.
questions.knowledgeNote: Le Chatelier's principle: added heat or pressure is countered by a shift towards the endothermic or less gaseous side.

questions.question: Explain Down's process for the extraction of sodium.
questions.solution:
**Down's process:** Electrolysis of molten NaCl (with CaCl₂ added to lower melting point from 801°C to ~600°C).

- Anode (graphite): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂↑ + 2e⁻
- Cathode (iron): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na↓
- Na metal collects under a steel bell
- CaCl₂ addition lowers melting point and increases conductivity
questions.knowledgeNote: Sodium cannot be extracted from aqueous solution because Na⁺ is harder to reduce than H₂O.

questions.question: Compare the extraction of sodium by the Downs cell with the extraction of magnesium by the electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride. Give the electrode reactions and state the physical state of each metal obtained.
questions.solution:
**Downs cell — sodium (NaCl melted with CaCl₂ at about 850 °C).**

Sodium is more reactive than magnesium, so its chloride must be reduced by electrolysis, not by carbon.

Cathode: $\text{Na}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Na}$. The working temperature of 850 °C is above the m.p. of sodium ($97.8$ °C), so **liquid sodium** floats up and is tapped through a separate pipe, away from the chlorine.

Anode: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^-$. Chlorine gas rises and escapes; the iron diaphragm prevents it from mixing with the sodium.

$$2\text{NaCl(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{Na(l)} + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

**Electrolysis of fused MgCl₂ (about 750 °C).**

Cathode: $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Mg}$. Magnesium melts at $650$ °C but the bath is kept hotter, so **solid magnesium** is deposited and scraped off, protecting it from further oxidation.

Anode: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^-$.

$$\text{MgCl}_2(l) \rightarrow \text{Mg(s)} + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

**Contrast.** Both need electrolysis of a fused (anhydrous) halide and both yield chlorine at the anode, but sodium is obtained as a liquid (higher operating temperature) whereas magnesium is obtained as a solid (lower operating temperature).
questions.knowledgeNote: Both metals are extracted by electrolysis of fused chlorides; sodium comes off liquid, magnesium as a solid.

questions.question: Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by carbon reduction of its oxide but is obtained by the electrolysis of a solution of alumina in molten cryolite. Give the relevant electrode reactions.
questions.solution:
**Why carbon reduction fails.**

The Gibbs energy of formation of $Al_2O_3$ is very negative (about $-1580$ kJ mol⁻¹), so aluminium is far below carbon in the Ellingham diagram. Carbon is not strong enough to reduce it, and any attempt needs temperatures at which the oxide itself would melt and decompose.

**The Hall–Héroult cell.**

Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite, $Na_3AlF_6$ (with $CaF_2$ as a flux). Cryolite lowers the fusion temperature from about $2072$ °C to about $950$ °C and improves conductivity, so much less heat is needed and molten aluminium (m.p. $660$ °C) is tapped off as liquid.

**Cathode (carbon lining) — reduction:**

$$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Al(l)}$$

**Anode (graphite rods) — oxidation of oxide ions, the carbon burns away:**

$$\text{C} + 2\text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 4e^-$$

**Overall:**

$$2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \rightarrow 4\text{Al} + 3\text{CO}_2$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Aluminium's oxide is too stable for carbon reduction, so Hall–Héroult electrolysis in molten cryolite is used instead.

questions.question: Arrange the oxoacids of chlorine HClO, HClO₂, HClO₃ and HClO₄ in order of increasing acid strength and explain the trend. ($K_a$: 3.0 × 10⁻⁸, 4.0 × 10⁻², 5 × 10¹, 10¹⁰)
questions.solution:
**Order of increasing acid strength:**

$$\text{HClO} < \text{HClO}_2 < \text{HClO}_3 < \text{HClO}_4$$

This matches the increase in $K_a$ from $3.0 \times 10^{-8}$ to $10^{10}$.

**Explanation.**

Each extra oxygen atom pulls electrons away from the O–H bond through its strong $-I$ inductive effect, so the O–H bond becomes weaker and the proton is lost more easily. The $O^-$ groups generated are also stabilised by resonance delocalisation over several oxygens, making the conjugate base more stable and the acid stronger.

Pauling's empirical rule, $pK_a \approx 8 - 5m$ where $m$ is the number of non-protonated oxygen atoms, confirms it: HClO ($m=0$) gives $pK_a \approx 8$; HClO₂ ($m=1$) $pK_a \approx 3$; HClO₃ ($m=2$) $pK_a \approx -2$; HClO₄ ($m=3$) $pK_a \approx -7$. Perchloric acid is thus one of the strongest acids known.
questions.knowledgeNote: Acid strength of oxoacids rises with each added oxygen because of the inductive effect and resonance stabilisation of the anion.

questions.question: Why is helium used in diving equipment instead of nitrogen?
questions.solution: Helium is less soluble in blood than nitrogen. Under high pressure, nitrogen dissolves in blood causing 'the bends' (decompression sickness). Helium's low solubility prevents this — divers use helium-oxygen mixtures.
questions.knowledgeNote: Helium is also used in deep-sea diving because it doesn't cause nitrogen narcosis.

questions.question: Describe the industrial preparation of nitric acid by the Ostwald process. Give balanced equations, the catalyst and the conditions used at each stage.
questions.solution:
**Stage 1 — Oxidation of ammonia (about 850 °C, finely divided platinum or platinum–rhodium gauze).**

$$4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow[\sim 850 \ ^\circ\text{C}]{\text{Pt}} 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Stage 2 — Oxidation of nitric oxide to nitrogen dioxide (about 50 °C, fast reaction, no catalyst needed).**

$$2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}_2$$

**Stage 3 — Absorption of nitrogen dioxide in water.**

$$3\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{HNO}_3 + \text{NO}$$

The nitric oxide formed again is re-oxidised to $NO_2$ and re-absorbed, so nearly all the nitrogen is converted to nitric acid. The overall reaction is

$$\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

The plant is cooled continuously because the reactions are strongly exothermic.
questions.knowledgeNote: Ostwald process: ammonia is oxidised over Pt at 850 °C, NO is oxidised to NO₂, then absorbed in water to give nitric acid.

questions.question: Identify the elements with atomic numbers 19, 20, 31, 36 and 55, and state the period and group in which each one is placed in the long form of the periodic table.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Number of electrons and period.**

The period number equals the number of electron shells (principal quantum number) occupied, i.e. the $n$ value of the outermost electron.

**Step 2 — Group number.**

For elements of $s$- and $p$-blocks, group number $= (number of valence electrons) + 10$.

| $Z$ | Element | Electronic configuration (outer part) | Period | Group |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 19 | Potassium (K) | $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^1$ | 4 | 1 |
| 20 | Calcium (Ca) | $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2$ | 4 | 2 |
| 31 | Gallium (Ga) | $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^24p^1$ | 4 | 13 |
| 36 | Krypton (Kr) | $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^24p^6$ | 4 | 18 |
| 55 | Caesium (Cs) | $[\text{Xe}]\,6s^1$ | 6 | 1 |

Notice that four of the five elements lie in period 4, whereas caesium (Z = 55) lies in period 6, showing that period length is not fixed.
questions.knowledgeNote: Period number equals the principal quantum number of the outermost electron, while group is decided by the valence electrons.
