questions.question: Differentiate between deviation of light and dispersion of light.
questions.solution:
**Deviation of light:** The bending of a single ray (or single colour) of light from its original straight path when it passes through a prism or a slab, by an angle $\delta$.
$$\delta = i + e - A$$
It occurs even for **monochromatic** light.

**Dispersion of light:** The splitting of white light into its constituent colours because different colours are deviated by different angles. It requires **polychromatic** (white) light.

**Key differences:** Deviation is a change in direction of one ray; dispersion is a separation of colours, so $\text{dispersion} > \text{deviation}$ for white light. A red glass slab disperses (gives colour) but a plain glass slab of same shape only deviates.
questions.knowledgeNote: Deviation bends a single ray of light; dispersion splits white light into colours due to varying refractive index.

questions.question: State Newton's three laws of motion. Give an example of each.
questions.solution:
**First Law (Inertia):** A body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion continues in a straight line at constant velocity unless acted on by an external force. *Example: passengers in a bus lurch forward when brakes are applied.*

**Second Law:** F = ma. *Example: a cricket ball accelerates when a bat applies force.*

**Third Law:** For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. *Example: a rocket pushes gas downward and is propelled upward.*
questions.knowledgeNote: The three laws hold in inertial frames only; the third implies momentum and force conservation.

questions.question: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a rough inclined plane of angle 30 degrees with the horizontal. If the coefficient of friction is 0.2, find the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the block.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Resolve the weight vertically and normally:**
$$N = mg\cos\theta = 10 \times 9.8 \times \cos 30^\circ = 98 \times 0.866$$
$$N = 84.87\ \text{N}$$

**Step 2 — Frictional force** (since the block rests, friction balances the downslope component):
$$F = \mu N = 0.2 \times 84.87$$
$$\boxed{F = \mathbf{16.97\ N} \approx \mathbf{17\ N}}$$

**Step 3 — Check:** The component of weight down the slope is
$$mg\sin 30^\circ = 10 \times 9.8 \times 0.5 = 49\ \text{N}$$
Since $49\ \text{N} > 17\ \text{N}$, friction is indeed sufficient to hold the block at rest, confirming the result.
questions.knowledgeNote: Friction equals mu times normal force, and on an incline the normal force equals mg cosine of the slope angle.

questions.question: Differentiate between mass and weight.
questions.solution:
**Mass:**
- The quantity of matter contained in a body; it is a **scalar** and a **fundamental quantity**.
- Measured in kilograms (kg); SI base unit of mass.
- It is **independent** of location, gravitational field and the state of motion.
- It is **invariant** everywhere in the universe.
- Invariant mass is given by $m_0 = \dfrac{m_{rel}}{\gamma}$.

**Weight:**
- The force with which the earth attracts a body; $W = mg$.
- It is a **vector** (directed towards the centre of the earth) and a **derived quantity**.
- Measured in newtons (N) or kilogram-force; SI unit is the newton.
- It **varies** with $g$, so it changes with latitude, altitude and the celestial body.
- On the moon, weight is one-sixth of that on the earth while mass is unchanged.

**Apparent weight** $W_{app} = mg - F_{centrifugal}$ can even be zero during free fall.
questions.knowledgeNote: Mass is invariant scalar matter measured in kg; weight is the gravitational force mg measured in newton and varies with g.

questions.question: Define stress, strain, and Young's modulus. What are their SI units?
questions.solution:
**Stress:** Force per unit area (F/A). SI unit: **Pascal (Pa)** = N/mÂ².
**Strain:** Fractional change in dimension (Î”L/L). SI unit: **dimensionless**.
**Young's modulus:** Ratio of stress to strain (Y = stress/strain). SI unit: **Pascal (Pa)**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Three elastic moduli: Young's modulus (tensile), Shear modulus (rigidity), Bulk modulus (compressibility). Steel has Y â‰ˆ 2Ã—10Â¹Â¹ Pa

questions.question: Define Young's modulus and write its formula and SI unit.
questions.solution:
**Definition:** Young's modulus is defined as the ratio of longitudinal stress (tensile force per unit area) to the corresponding longitudinal strain (extension per unit original length) within the **elastic limit**.

**Formula:**
$$Y = \frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \frac{\dfrac{F}{A}}{\dfrac{\Delta L}{L}} = \boxed{\frac{FL}{A\Delta L}}$$
where $F$ = tensile force, $A$ = cross-sectional area, $L$ = original length, $\Delta L$ = extension.

**SI unit:** $\text{N m}^{-2}$ (pascal). Dimensional formula: $\left[ML^{-1}T^{-2}\right]$.

**Significance:** A large Young's modulus means the material is stiff and resists deformation. Steel: $\sim 2 \times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}$; rubber: $\sim 5 \times 10^6\ \text{Pa}$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Young's modulus is stress divided by strain, measured in pascals; high values indicate a stiff, rigid material.

questions.question: A copper wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area $2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2$ is stretched by 2 mm when a force of 200 N is applied. Find Young's modulus of copper.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given and converted to SI:**
$F = 200\ \text{N},\ L = 2\ \text{m},\ A = 2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2,\ \Delta L = 2\ \text{mm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}$

**Step 2 — Young's modulus:**

**Step 3 — Substitute:**

**Verification:** Stress $= 200/2\times10^{-5} = 1 \times 10^{7}\ \text{Pa}$; Strain $= 2\times10^{-3}/2 = 1 \times 10^{-3}$.
$$Y = \frac{10^{7}}{10^{-3}} = 10^{10}\ \text{Pa}$$ ✓

questions.question: What is meant by quantisation of electric charge? Explain why a charge of 2.5 e can never be observed.
questions.solution:
**Quantisation of charge:** All electric charges are always an **integer multiple** of the elementary charge $e$. That is, $q = ne$, where $n$ is any integer (positive, negative or zero).
$$e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$$
**So possible charges are:** $\ldots, -3e, -2e, -e, 0, +e, +2e, +3e, \ldots$ — the value $0.5e$ or $2.5e$ can never occur.

**Reason:** Charge is carried by **quark** particles inside protons and neutrons. Quarks carry fractional charges ($\pm e/3$ and $\pm 2e/3$) but quarks are **never found free** in nature — they are always bound in pairs or triplets of colour-neutral hadrons. Hence every observable particle (proton, neutron, electron) carries an **integral** multiple of $e$.

This is why the electrical charge is said to be **quantised**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Charge is quantised because free quarks never appear alone, so all observable charges are integer multiples of the elementary charge.

questions.question: Find the electric field intensity at a point 2 m from a point charge of +4 microC. Take $k = 9 \times 10^9\ \text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $q = 4 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C},\ r = 2\ \text{m}$

**Step 2 — Electric field intensity due to a point charge:**
$$E = \frac{kq}{r^2} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(4 \times 10^{-6})}{(2)^2}$$
$$E = \frac{36 \times 10^3}{4}$$
$$\boxed{E = \mathbf{9 \times 10^3\ \text{N/C}}$$

**Step 3 — Direction:** The charge is positive, so the field is directed **radially outward** from the charge.

**Step 4 — Alternative form using force on a test charge:**
$$\text{If } q_0 = 1\ \mu\text{C}, \quad F = kq q_0/r^2 = 9\times10^9 \times 4\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}/4 = 9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}$$
$$E = \frac{F}{q_0} = \frac{9 \times 10^{-3}}{10^{-6}} = 9 \times 10^3\ \text{N/C}$$ ✓

questions.question: Two equal charges of +2 microC each are placed 10 cm apart. Find the electric field intensity at the midpoint of the line joining them.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Geometry:** The charges are $10\ \text{cm}$ apart, so the midpoint is $r = 5\ \text{cm} = 0.05\ \text{m}$ from each charge.

**Step 2 — Field due to one charge at the midpoint:**
$$E_1 = \frac{kq}{r^2} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(2 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.05)^2} = \frac{18 \times 10^3}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}}$$
$$E_1 = \mathbf{7.2 \times 10^6\ \text{N/C}}$$

**Step 3 — Field due to the other charge:**
$$E_2 = E_1 = 7.2 \times 10^6\ \text{N/C}$$

**Step 4 — Directions:** At the midpoint, $E_1$ acts **away from** the first positive charge (to the right) while $E_2$ acts **away from** the second (to the left). The two fields are **equal in magnitude but opposite in direction**, so they cancel.

$$\boxed{E_{net} = E_2 - E_1 = 7.2\times10^6 - 7.2\times10^6 = \mathbf{0}}$$
**The electric field at the midpoint of the line joining two equal like charges is zero.**
questions.knowledgeNote: At the midpoint between two equal like charges the fields are equal and opposite, so the net field is zero.

questions.question: State the concept of escape velocity. Calculate the escape velocity from the surface of a planet whose surface gravity is 5 m/s2 and radius is $6 \times 10^6$ m.
questions.solution:
**Escape velocity:** The escape velocity of a planet is the minimum velocity with which a body must be projected from the surface so that it **escapes the gravitational field** of the planet and never returns.

**Derivation:** If a body of mass $m$ is projected with velocity $v_e$, the total energy at the surface is
$$\frac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R}$$
For the body to just escape, this energy must be **zero** at infinity:
$$\frac{1}{2}mv_e^2 = \frac{GMm}{R} \Rightarrow v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}$$
Since $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, we have $GM = gR^2$, hence
$$\boxed{v_e = \sqrt{2gR}}$$

**Numerical:**
$$v_e = \sqrt{2 \times 5 \times 6 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{6 \times 10^7}$$
$$\boxed{v_e \approx 7.75 \times 10^3\ \text{m/s}}$$

(Also $v_e = \sqrt{2}\,v_{orb}$.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Escape velocity is the root of 2gR, the minimum speed needed for a body to leave a planet's gravitational field.

questions.question: The mass of a planet is 8 times that of the earth and its radius is twice that of the earth. Find the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the planet. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Acceleration due to gravity at the surface:**
$$g = \frac{GM}{R^2}$$

**Step 2 — For the planet:**
$$g_p = \frac{G(8M)}{(2R)^2} = \frac{8GM}{4R^2} = 2\left(\frac{GM}{R^2}\right) = 2g$$

**Step 3 — Result:**
$$\boxed{g_p = 2 \times 9.8 = \mathbf{19.6\ \text{m/s}^2}}$$

**Note on the density:** $\rho = \dfrac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$, so $\dfrac{\rho_p}{\rho_e} = \dfrac{8}{8} = 1$. The planet has the **same density** as the earth, hence the same gravitational field at the surface.
questions.knowledgeNote: Surface gravity scales as mass divided by radius squared, so eight times the mass at twice the radius doubles g.

questions.question: State and explain the zeroth law of thermodynamics. Why is it called the zeroth law?
questions.solution: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. It is called the 'zeroth' law because it logically precedes the first and second laws, and was recognized after them but is more fundamental â€” hence 'zero'.
questions.knowledgeNote: The zeroth law defines temperature and thermal equilibrium. It is the basis for temperature measurement.

questions.question: A thermometer reads -5 degrees C when placed in ice water and 105 degrees C in boiling water. What reading does it give when placed in liquid at 40 degrees C?
questions.solution:
Assume the thermometer scale is linear: $R = mT + c$.

**Step 1 — Two calibration points:**
$T = 0^\circ\text{C} \Rightarrow R = -5$
$T = 100^\circ\text{C} \Rightarrow R = 105$

**Step 2 — Slope of the scale:**
$$m = \frac{105 - (-5)}{100 - 0} = \frac{110}{100} = 1.1$$

**Step 3 — Intercept:**
$$-5 = 1.1(0) + c \;\Rightarrow\; c = -5$$
So the relation is $R = 1.1T - 5$.

**Step 4 — Reading at $T = 40^\circ\text{C}$:**
$$R = 1.1 \times 40 - 5 = 44 - 5$$
$$\boxed{R = \mathbf{39^\circ\text{C}}}$$

**Verification by interpolation:** rise in reading $= -5 + (40 - 0) \times \frac{110}{100} = -5 + 44 = 39$ ✓
Since the slope exceeds 1, this is a 'fool' or inaccurate thermometer.
questions.knowledgeNote: For a linear thermometer scale, interpolation between ice and steam points gives the intermediate reading.

questions.question: What is the difference between heat and temperature? Give their SI units.
questions.solution:
Heat is the energy transferred between systems due to temperature difference. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles.

**Heat:** SI unit = **Joule (J)** (energy transfer).
**Temperature:** SI unit = **Kelvin (K)**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Heat is a mode of transfer; temperature is the degree of hotness measured by a thermometer.

questions.question: Differentiate between heat and temperature.
questions.solution:
**Heat:**
- A form of **energy** in transit transferred from one body to another due to a temperature difference.
- It is an **extensive** quantity and is measured in **joule (J)** or calorie.
- It flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature.
- $Q = mc\Delta T$; heat added or removed changes the temperature.
- It is a **process** quantity, not stored in a body.

**Temperature:**
- The **degree of hotness or coldness** of a body; a measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules.
- It is an **intensive** quantity, independent of the amount of substance.
- It is measured in **kelvin (K)** or degree Celsius.
- It is a **state** function: a body has a definite temperature at a given state.
- It determines the **direction** of heat flow.

**Note:** Large bodies can have a high temperature but contain little heat, and small bodies can contain much heat at a low temperature.
questions.knowledgeNote: Heat is energy transferred due to temperature difference, extensive and measured in joules; temperature is hotness, intensive and in kelvin.

questions.question: State the kinetic theory of gases. Also state its assumptions.
questions.solution:
**Kinetic theory:** Gas pressure arises from molecular collisions with container walls. The pressure is proportional to the average kinetic energy of molecules.

**Assumptions:**
1. Gas consists of many molecules in random motion.
2. Molecules are point particles with negligible volume.
3. No intermolecular forces between molecules (except during collisions).
4. Collisions are perfectly elastic (no KE loss).
5. Time of collision is negligible compared to time between collisions.
6. Molecules move with constant velocity between collisions.
questions.knowledgeNote: From kinetic theory: PV = (1/3)NmâŸ¨vÂ²âŸ©. Combining with ideal gas law gives KE = (3/2)kT â€” average KE per degree of freedom.

questions.question: A gas at 27 degrees C and pressure $1.0 \times 10^5$ Pa occupies a volume of 0.5 cubic metre. Find its volume at 100 degrees C if the pressure remains constant. Take atmospheric pressure as $1.01 \times 10^5$ Pa.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Convert to absolute (kelvin) temperature:**
$$T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\ \text{K}, \qquad T_2 = 100 + 273 = 373\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — Charles's law** (pressure constant):
$$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2} \;\Rightarrow\; V_2 = V_1\,\frac{T_2}{T_1}$$

**Step 3 — Substitute:**
$$V_2 = 0.5 \times \frac{373}{300} = \frac{186.5}{300}$$
$$\boxed{V_2 = \mathbf{0.402\ \text{m}^3}}$$

**Step 4 — Interpretation:** The volume **increases** (from 0.5 to 0.402... i.e. it changes) as the absolute temperature rises, since $T_2 > T_1$.

**Step 5 — Coefficient of expansivity check:**
$$\gamma = \frac{\Delta V}{V_0\Delta T} = \frac{(0.5 - 0.402)}{0.402 \times 73} = \frac{0.098}{29.3} \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{K}^{-1}$$
This is close to $1/273\ \text{K}^{-1} \approx 3.66 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, the value for an ideal gas.
questions.knowledgeNote: At constant pressure volume varies directly with absolute temperature, so 0.5 cubic metres at 300 K becomes 0.402 at 373 K.

questions.question: What is the law of equipartition of energy? How many degrees of freedom does a monoatomic gas molecule have?
questions.solution:
The law states that energy is equally divided among all available degrees of freedom, each getting (1/2)kT of energy.

A monoatomic gas molecule has **3 translational degrees of freedom** (motion along x, y, z). Its molar specific heat at constant volume: Cv = (3/2)R.
questions.knowledgeNote: At thermal equilibrium, a monatomic gas has 3 translational degrees of freedom, a diatomic gas 5.

questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles's law and explain them with the $\mu$ notation.
questions.solution:
**Boyle's law:** At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is **inversely proportional** to its volume.
$$P \propto \frac{1}{V} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{PV = \text{constant}} \;\Rightarrow\; P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$$
Graph of $P$ vs $V$ is a **rectangular hyperbola**; pressure increases when volume decreases. Follows Boyle's law $P \propto 1/V$; used in breathing and in the piston of an engine.

**Charles's law:** At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is **directly proportional** to its absolute temperature.
$$V \propto T \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\frac{V}{T} = \text{constant}} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$$
Graph of $V$ vs $T$ is a **straight line through the origin**; the slope of $V$ vs $T$ (K) is the coefficient of cubical expansivity $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V_0}\left(\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta T}\right)$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Boyle's law gives PV constant at constant temperature; Charles's law gives V proportional to T at constant pressure.

questions.question: A car moving at 10 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s2 for 4 s. Find the final velocity and the distance travelled in this time.
questions.solution:
**Given:** $u = 10\ \text{m/s},\ a = 2\ \text{m/s}^2,\ t = 4\ \text{s}$

**Step 1 — Final velocity:**
$$v = u + at = 10 + (2)(4) = 10 + 8$$
$$\boxed{v = \mathbf{18\ \text{m/s}}$$

**Step 2 — Distance travelled:**
Using $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$:
$$s = (10)(4) + \frac{1}{2}(2)(16) = 40 + 16$$
$$\boxed{s = \mathbf{56\ \text{m}}$$

**Step 3 — Verification** using the average velocity rule:
$$s = \frac{u + v}{2}\times t = \frac{10 + 18}{2} \times 4 = 14 \times 4 = 56\ \text{m}$$ ✓

**Average speed** $= 56/4 = \mathbf{14\ \text{m/s}}$ (equal to $\tfrac{u+v}{2}$ for uniform acceleration).
questions.knowledgeNote: For uniform acceleration, v equals u plus at and distance equals ut plus half at squared.

questions.question: A stone is projected vertically upwards with a velocity of 49 m/s. Taking $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, find the time taken to reach maximum height, the maximum height and the total time of flight. Ignore air resistance.
questions.solution:
**Given:** $u = 49\ \text{m/s},\ g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ (upward positive, so $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$)

**Step 1 — Time to reach maximum height:**
At maximum height the vertical velocity becomes zero, $v = 0$.
$$v = u + at \;\Rightarrow\; 0 = 49 - 9.8t$$
$$\boxed{t = 5\ \text{s}}$$

**Step 2 — Maximum height:**
$$h = u t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 49 \times 5 - \frac{1}{2}(9.8)(25) = 245 - 122.5$$
$$\boxed{h = 122.5\ \text{m}}$$
(Equivalently $h = u^2/2g = 2401/19.6 = 122.5\ \text{m}$ ✓)

**Step 3 — Total time of flight** (time up equals time down by symmetry):
$$\boxed{T = 2t = 10\ \text{s}}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: For vertical projection, time to reach the top is u over g, max height is u squared over 2g, and flight time is twice that.

questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 15 cm forms a real image which is twice the size of the object. Find the positions of the object and the image and the magnification.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Sign of magnification:**
Since the image is **real**, it is inverted, so $m$ is negative:
$$m = -\frac{v}{u} = -2 \;\Rightarrow\; v = 2u$$

**Step 2 — Lens formula** with $f = +15\ \text{cm}$:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
$$\frac{1}{2u} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{15}$$
$$-\frac{1}{2u} = \frac{1}{15} \Rightarrow 2u = -15$$
$$\boxed{u = -7.5\ \text{cm}}$$

**Step 3 — Image position:**
$$v = 2u = 2 \times (-7.5)$$
$$\boxed{v = -15\ \text{cm}}$$

**Step 4 — Magnification:**
$$m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-15}{-7.5} = \mathbf{-2}$$

**Step 5 — Verification with the lens formula:**
$$\frac{1}{-15} - \frac{1}{-7.5} = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{2}{15} = \frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{f}$$ ✓

**Nature:** Real, inverted and magnified (twice the object). The object lies between $f$ and $2f$, and the image is formed beyond $2f$.
questions.knowledgeNote: A convex lens giving a real image twice the size has the object between f and 2f and the image beyond 2f.

questions.question: State the thin lens maker's formula. Derive it for a convex lens.
questions.solution:
**Lens maker's formula:** 1/f = (μ-1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂)

Derivation: Using refraction at two spherical surfaces and applying sign convention for thin lens:
For first surface: (μ-1)/R₁ contribution
For second surface: -(μ-1)/R₂ contribution
Adding: 1/f = (μ-1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂)

Where μ = refractive index of lens material, R₁ and R₂ are radii of curvature of the two surfaces.
questions.knowledgeNote: For a double convex lens with equal radii R: 1/f = 2(μ-1)/R

questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg moving under a constant net force changes its velocity from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Calculate the force acting on it.
questions.solution:

**Step 2 — Newton's second law:**
$$F = ma = 5 \times 2$$

**Step 3 — Result:**
$$F = \mathbf{10\ \text{N}}$$
The force acts in the direction of motion of the body.

questions.question: A bullet of mass 0.02 kg moving with a velocity of 500 m/s is embedded in a block of mass 4.98 kg initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. Find the velocity of the combined system.
questions.solution:
**Given:** $m_1 = 0.02\ \text{kg},\ u_1 = 500\ \text{m/s},\ m_2 = 4.98\ \text{kg},\ u_2 = 0$

**Step 1 — Apply conservation of momentum** (no external horizontal force):
$$m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v$$

**Step 2 — Substitute values:**
$$0.02 \times 500 + 4.98 \times 0 = (0.02 + 4.98)v$$
$$10 = 5.0\,v$$

**Step 3 — Solve:**
$$v = \frac{10}{5.0} = \mathbf{2.0\ \text{m/s}}$$
The direction is that of the bullet's initial motion.
questions.knowledgeNote: In a perfectly inelastic collision the colliding bodies stick together and share a common velocity from momentum conservation.

questions.question: State Newton's three laws of motion.
questions.solution:
**First law (law of inertia):** Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to change its state.

**Second law:** The rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the net external force, and the acceleration is in the direction of that force.
$$F = ma = m\left(\frac{v - u}{t}\right)$$

**Third law (action and reaction):** To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, and the two forces always act on two **different** bodies, so they never cancel each other.
questions.knowledgeNote: Newton's three laws cover inertia, the proportionality F = ma, and equal-and-opposite action-reaction pairs on separate bodies.

questions.question: Differentiate between elastic and inelastic collisions.
questions.solution:
**Elastic collision:** Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, the bodies move separately after collision, no heat, sound or deformation is produced, and total kinetic energy is unchanged.

**Inelastic collision:** Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is **not** conserved; part of it is converted into heat, sound and deformation. If the bodies stick together after impact it is called a **perfectly inelastic** collision, and by the law of conservation of energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)V^2$ holds.

**Example:** Collision of two steel balls is elastic; a bullet embedded in a wooden block is perfectly inelastic.
questions.knowledgeNote: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy; inelastic ones conserve only momentum.

questions.question: Define radioactive decay constant. Write the relation between half-life and decay constant.
questions.solution:
**Decay constant (λ):** Probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay.

Half-life: T₁/₂ = ln(2)/λ = 0.693/λ

Mean life: τ = 1/λ = T₁/₂/ln(2)
questions.knowledgeNote: Radioactive decay is random but predictable statistically. After n half-lives: N = N₀(1/2)ⁿ

questions.question: What is mass defect? How is it related to binding energy?
questions.solution:
**Mass defect (Δm):** The difference between the sum of masses of individual nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus.

Δm = [Zmp + (A-Z)mn] - M(nucleus)

**Binding energy:** The energy equivalent of mass defect: E = Δm × c²

Higher binding energy per nucleon → more stable nucleus.
questions.knowledgeNote: Binding energy per nucleon is maximum (~8.7 MeV) for iron-56. Heavier nuclei release energy by fission; lighter nuclei by fusion.

questions.question: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of the sample remains after 24 days, and what will be its activity if the initial activity was 4 curie?
questions.solution:
**Definition of half-life:** The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time required for **half** of its initial number of atoms to decay, or equivalently for its activity to become half of the original value.

**Step 1 — Number of half-lives elapsed:**
$$n = \frac{24\ \text{days}}{8\ \text{days}} = 3$$

**Step 2 — Fraction of the sample remaining:**
$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}$$
$$\boxed{\text{Fraction remaining} = \mathbf{\dfrac{1}{8}}\ (=12.5\%)}$$

**Step 3 — Activity after 24 days:**
Activity falls by half each half-life, so
$$A = \frac{4}{2^3} = \frac{4}{8}$$
$$\boxed{A = \mathbf{0.5\ \text{curie}}$$

**Note:** $1\ \text{curie} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}$ decays per second, so the final activity is $1.85 \times 10^{10}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
questions.knowledgeNote: After three half-lives of eight days each, one-eighth of the sample remains and the activity falls from 4 to 0.5 curie.

questions.question: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion with one example each.
questions.solution:
**Nuclear fission:** A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy.
Example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + energy (used in nuclear reactors)

**Nuclear fusion:** Two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
Example: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + energy (powers the sun and hydrogen bombs)
questions.knowledgeNote: Fission requires critical mass; fusion requires extremely high temperature (~10⁷ K). Fusion releases more energy per kg than fission.

questions.question: After n half-lives the fraction of radioactive atoms remaining is: (a) 1/2 to the power n (b) n/2 (c) 2 to the power n (d) 1 over n squared
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (a) $1/2^n$.**

**Step 1:** In each half-life the number of undecayed atoms becomes half of the previous value.
After 1 half-life: $N = N_0/2$
After 2 half-lives: $N = N_0/4$
After 3 half-lives: $N = N_0/8$

**Step 2 — Generalising:**
$$N = N_0\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \Rightarrow \frac{N}{N_0} = \boxed{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n = \frac{1}{2^n}}$$

**Check:** For $n = 3$, the fraction is $1/8$ ✓, and the activity follows exactly the same law.
Hence options (b), (c) and (d) are incorrect.
questions.knowledgeNote: The fraction of radioactive atoms remaining after n half-lives is one over two to the power n.

questions.question: What is meant by total internal reflection? State the conditions for it to occur and write the relation between refractive index and critical angle.
questions.solution:
**Total internal reflection (TIR):** The phenomenon in which a ray of light travelling from a denser medium to a rarer medium is completely reflected back into the denser medium, without any refraction, is called total internal reflection.

**Conditions:**
1. Light must travel from a **denser** to a **rarer** medium ($\mu_1 > \mu_2$).
2. The angle of incidence must be **greater than the critical angle** $C$.

**Relation:** At the critical angle $C$, $r = 90^\circ$, so by the law of refraction
$$\mu_1 = \mu_2\,\frac{\sin 90^\circ}{\sin C} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\mu = \frac{1}{\sin C}}$$

**Examples:** TIR in a glass slab, sparkle of a diamond, mirage, and total internal reflection in optical fibres.
questions.knowledgeNote: TIR needs a denser-to-rarer medium with incidence angle exceeding critical angle, where mu equals one over sin C.

questions.question: Differentiate between a real image and a virtual image.
questions.solution:
**Real image:** Formed when the reflected or refracted rays actually **converge** at a point.
- It can be obtained on a screen and is **inverted** (laterally inverted).
- Magnification $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$ is negative.
- Formed by concave mirrors, convex lenses, and plane mirrors of object and image on the same side is not possible.
- $v$ and $u$ have opposite signs under Cartesian convention.

**Virtual image:** Formed when the reflected or refracted rays appear to **diverge** from a point and meet only on extension behind the mirror or lens.
- **Cannot** be obtained on a screen.
- Erect and same size as object for a plane mirror.
- Magnification is positive.
- $u$ and $v$ have the **same** sign.
questions.knowledgeNote: A real image is formed by actual convergence and is screenable; a virtual image only appears on ray extension.

questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms an image of an object placed 60 cm from the lens on the principal axis. Find the position and magnification of the image and state its nature.
questions.solution:
**Given:** $f = +20\ \text{cm},\ u = -60\ \text{cm}$

**Step 1 — Lens formula** (new Cartesian sign convention):
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{-60} = \frac{1}{20}$$
$$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{60} = \frac{3}{60}$$
$$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{3 - 1}{60} = \frac{2}{60} = \frac{1}{30}$$

**Step 2 — Image position:**
$$v = \mathbf{+30\ \text{cm}}$$
So the image is formed 30 cm on the **other side** of the lens.

**Step 3 — Magnification:**
$$m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{30}{-60} = \mathbf{-0.5}$$

**Step 4 — Nature:** $v$ is positive so the image is **real**; $m < 1$ so it is **diminished**, and $m < 0$ so it is **inverted**.

(Here the object lies between $f$ and $2f$, as expected.)
questions.knowledgeNote: For an object between f and 2f of a convex lens, the real image lies beyond 2f and is inverted and magnified.

questions.question: What is meant by the optical power of a lens? Write its SI unit.
questions.solution:
**Definition:** The optical power of a lens is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length when the focal length is expressed in **metres**.
$$\boxed{P = \frac{1}{f\ (\text{in m)}}\qquad \text{or} \qquad P = \frac{1000}{f\ (\text{in cm})}$$

**SI unit:** $\text{m}^{-1}$, also called the **dioptre (D)**.

**Sign:** Power is positive for a convex (converging) lens and negative for a concave (diverging) lens.

**Example:** A convex lens of focal length 50 cm has $P = \dfrac{1}{0.5} = +2\ \text{D}$. A lens of power $-4\ \text{D}$ has $f = -0.25\ \text{m} = -25\ \text{cm}$, i.e. a concave lens.
questions.knowledgeNote: Optical power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres, measured in dioptre or per metre.

questions.question: What is the difference between accuracy and precision? Illustrate with an example.
questions.solution:
**Accuracy** = how close a measurement is to the true value; **Precision** = how close repeated measurements are to each other.

Example: A dartboard â€” if all darts cluster near the bullseye, the throws are both accurate and precise. If they cluster far from the bullseye, they are precise but inaccurate. If they are scattered widely around the bullseye, they are accurate on average but not precise.
questions.knowledgeNote: Accuracy relates to systematic error; precision relates to random error. More measurements improve precision but not accuracy.

questions.question: Write any four fundamental quantities with their SI units and define the SI unit of mass.
questions.solution:
**Four fundamental quantities and SI units:**

| Quantity | SI unit |
|---|---|
| Length | metre (m) |
| Mass | kilogram (kg) |
| Time | second (s) |
| Electric current | ampere (A) |

(Other fundamental quantities are thermodynamic temperature in kelvin (K), luminous intensity in candela (cd) and amount of substance in mole (mol).)

**Definition of the unit of mass:** The **kilogram** is the unit of mass. It is defined as the mass of a prototype cylinder of platinum-iridium (90% platinum, 10% iridium) kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) at Sèvres, France.

$1\ \text{kg} = \dfrac{1}{1000}\ \text{grams}$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Mass is a fundamental quantity measured in kilogram, historically defined by an international platinum-iridium prototype cylinder.

questions.question: The SI dimensional unit kg m2 s-2 represents: (a) work (b) force (c) power (d) impulse
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (a) work.**

**Step 1 — Check each quantity:**
- Force: $F = ma = \text{kg m s}^{-2}$ — does **not** match.
- Work: $W = Fs = \text{kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{m} = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}$ — **matches**. ✓
- Power: $P = W/t = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-3}$ — does not match.
- Impulse: $Ft = \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ — does not match.

**Step 2 — Conclusion:** $\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2} = \text{N m} = \text{J}$, so it is **work (and energy)**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Kilogram metre squared per second squared equals newton metre, which is the joule used for work and energy.

questions.question: One volt is equal to: (a) 1 joule (b) 1 joule per coulomb (c) 1 newton (d) 1 ampere
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (b) 1 joule per coulomb.**

One volt is defined as the potential difference between two points when one joule of work is done in bringing one coulomb of positive charge from one point to the other.
$$1\ \text{volt} = \frac{1\ \text{joule}}{1\ \text{coulomb}} = 1\ \text{V}$$
Its dimensions are $[M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-1}]$.
questions.knowledgeNote: One volt equals one joule of work done per coulomb of charge moved.

questions.question: Derive the relation between work done $W$, potential difference $V$ and the number of electrons $n$ flowing in a circuit.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Potential difference:** Work done in moving a charge $q$ through a potential difference $V$ is
$$W = qV$$

**Step 2 — Charge carried by n electrons:**
The charge on one electron is $-e$ where $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$, so the magnitude of charge carried by $n$ electrons is
$$q = ne = ne \quad \text{(magnitude)}
$$

**Step 3 — Substituting:**
$$\boxed{W = neV}\quad\text{or}\quad \boxed{V = \frac{W}{ne}}$$

**Step 4 — In terms of current** (current $I = q/t$):
$$W = neV = VIt$$

**Check:** If $W = 1\ \text{J}$, $n = 6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons and $V = 1\ \text{V}$, then $W = 6.25\times10^{18} \times 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 1 = 1\ \text{J}$. ✓
questions.knowledgeNote: Work equals the number of electrons times electronic charge times potential difference: W = neV.

questions.question: Define electric potential and electric potential difference. Write their SI units.
questions.solution:
**Electric potential:** The electric potential at a point in an electric field is the amount of work done in bringing a **unit positive charge** from infinity to that point without acceleration.
$$V = \frac{W}{q}\qquad \text{SI unit: volt (V, J C}^{-1}\text{)}$$
It is a **scalar** quantity.

**Electric potential difference:** The potential difference between two points $A$ and $B$ is the work done in taking a unit positive charge from $A$ to $B$.
$$V_{AB} = V_B - V_A = \frac{W_{AB}}{q}$$

Equipotential surfaces have the **same** potential. Potential is zero at infinity and is **always** positive for a positive charge.
questions.knowledgeNote: Electric potential is work done per unit positive charge brought from infinity, measured in volts.

questions.question: Find the work done in moving a charge of $2 \times 10^{-19}$ C through a potential difference of 300 V. Express the answer in electron volts.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Work done:**
$$W = qV = 2 \times 10^{-19} \times 300 = \mathbf{6.0 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{J}}$$

**Step 2 — Convert to electron volts:**
$$1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$
$$W = \frac{6.0 \times 10^{-17}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = \frac{6.0}{1.6} \times 10^{2}$$
$$W = \mathbf{375\ \text{eV}}$$

**Note:** The work done in moving one electron through 1 V is 1 eV, so $W\ (\text{eV}) = V$ (in volts) for a single electron.
questions.knowledgeNote: Work in joules is qV, and dividing by 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen joules converts it to electron volts.

questions.question: What is latent heat? Distinguish between latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization.
questions.solution:
Latent heat is the heat required to change the state of a unit mass of a substance without changing its temperature.

**Latent heat of fusion (Lf):** Heat to change 1 kg solid â†’ liquid (melting). Lf for ice = 334 kJ/kg.
**Latent heat of vaporization (Lv):** Heat to change 1 kg liquid â†’ gas (boiling). Lv for water = 2260 kJ/kg.
questions.knowledgeNote: Lv > Lf because vaporization requires breaking all intermolecular bonds, while fusion only breaks some.

questions.question: Define quantity of heat and specific heat capacity. Write the formula for the heat required to raise the temperature of a body and give the SI unit of specific heat capacity.
questions.solution:
**Quantity of heat:** The amount of heat $Q$ supplied to a body is the mass of the body multiplied by its specific heat capacity and the rise in temperature.
$$Q = mc\Delta T$$

**Specific heat capacity (c):** The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of **unit mass** of a substance by **one degree Celsius** (or one kelvin).
$$c = \frac{Q}{m\Delta T}$$

**SI unit:** $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ (also $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$). Dimensional formula: $\left[LT^{-2}\right]$.

**Values:** Water $= 4.2 \times 10^3\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ (maximum), ice $= 3.36 \times 10^3$, aluminium $= 0.9 \times 10^3$, copper $= 0.39 \times 10^3$, lead $= 0.13 \times 10^3$, mercury $= 0.14 \times 10^3$.

The large value for water is why water is an excellent coolant and why a hot bottle stays hot for long.
questions.knowledgeNote: Heat equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature rise; specific heat capacity has SI unit J per kg per K.

questions.question: Calculate the heat required to raise the temperature of 500 g of water from 20 degrees C to 60 degrees C. Take specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J/kg K.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $m = 500\ \text{g} = 0.5\ \text{kg},\ c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
$$\Delta T = 60 - 20 = 40\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — Heat required:**
$$Q = mc\Delta T = 0.5 \times 4200 \times 40$$
$$Q = 2100 \times 40$$
$$\boxed{Q = \mathbf{8.4 \times 10^4\ \text{J}} = \mathbf{84\ kJ}}$$

**Step 3 — In calories** (using $1\ \text{cal} = 4.2\ \text{J}$):
$$Q = \frac{8.4 \times 10^4}{4.2} = 2.0 \times 10^4\ \text{cal} = 20\ \text{kcal}$$

**Check:** Doubling the mass ($m \propto Q$) while keeping the temperature rise the same doubles the heat needed, which is consistent.
questions.knowledgeNote: Heat needed is mass times specific heat times temperature rise; 0.5 kg water through 40 K needs 84000 joules.

questions.question: A heater supplies 4200 J of heat to a body in 4 s. Calculate the rate of heat flow and state its SI unit.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $Q = 4200\ \text{J},\ t = 4\ \text{s}$

**Step 2 — Rate of heat flow:**
$$H = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{4200}{4}$$
$$\boxed{H = \mathbf{1050\ \text{W}}$$

**Step 3 — SI unit:** The SI unit is **watt (W)**, defined as one joule per second.
$$\text{Verification: } \frac{4200\ \text{J}}{4\ \text{s}} = 1050\ \text{J/s} = 1050\ \text{W}$$

questions.question: Define the rate of flow of heat. Write its formula and SI unit.
questions.solution:
**Definition:** The rate of flow of heat (heat current) is defined as the amount of heat flowing through a cross-section per unit time.
$$\boxed{\text{Rate of heat flow} = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}}$$

**SI unit:** $\text{J s}^{-1} = $ watt (W). The cgs unit is **calorie per second (cal/s)**.

**Note:** The rate at which heat flows is directly proportional to the temperature difference. If $Q$ is in joules and $t$ in seconds, $H = Q/t$ in watts; the rate per unit area is the **heat current density** in $\text{W m}^{-2}$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Rate of heat flow is heat divided by time, measured in watts (joules per second).

questions.question: Derive Newton's law of cooling.
questions.solution:
**Statement:** For a hot body cooling in air, the rate of loss of heat is directly proportional to the excess of temperature of the body over the surrounding temperature.

**Derivation:**
Let $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$ be the rate of cooling and $(\theta - \theta_0)$ the excess of temperature, where $\theta$ is the body's temperature and $\theta_0$ that of the surroundings.
At instant I: $\left(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right)_1 = k(\theta_1 - \theta_0)$
At instant II: $\left(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right)_2 = k(\theta_2 - \theta_0)$

**Dividing the two equations:**
$$\frac{(dQ/dt)_1}{(dQ/dt)_2} = \frac{\theta_1 - \theta_0}{\theta_2 - \theta_0}$$
$$\boxed{\text{Rate of cooling} \propto \text{excess of temperature over surroundings}}$$
This law holds only for small differences of temperature; Stefan's law applies in general.
questions.knowledgeNote: Newton's law of cooling states rate of heat loss is proportional to excess temperature over surroundings.

questions.question: What is superconductivity? State two properties of a superconductor and name one material that becomes superconducting.
questions.solution:
**Superconductivity:** It is the phenomenon in which the **electrical resistance of a material becomes exactly zero** and it becomes a perfect conductor when it is cooled below a certain critical temperature $T_c$. Below $T_c$ the material is said to be in the superconducting state.

**Properties:**
1. **Zero resistance:** A current once set up in a superconducting loop flows **indefinitely** without decaying, so no energy is lost as heat. Superconducting magnets can therefore produce very strong fields.
2. **Meissner effect:** A superconductor **expels all magnetic flux** from its interior when cooled below $T_c$ (perfect diamagnetism).

**Materials:** **Mercury** becomes superconducting at about **4.2 K** (the first known superconductor), and lead, tin, aluminium and niobium also become superconducting at low temperatures.

**Applications:** Magnetic levitation (maglev trains), MRI scanners, particle accelerators (CERN), SQUID magnetometers, and ultrasensitive power cables.
questions.knowledgeNote: Superconductivity means zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature, with magnetic flux expulsion from the material.

questions.question: What are elementary particles? List the four fundamental forces in order of decreasing strength.
questions.solution:
**Elementary particles:** Particles not made of smaller constituents — quarks, leptons, and gauge bosons.

Four fundamental forces (decreasing strength):
1. Strong nuclear force
2. Electromagnetic force
3. Weak nuclear force
4. Gravitational force
questions.knowledgeNote: Strong force: holds quarks together. EM force: acts on charged particles. Weak force: responsible for beta decay. Gravity: acts on all mass.

questions.question: Explain the working of a ruby laser with the help of a diagram and write any three uses of lasers.
questions.solution:
**Principle (three-level laser):** A ruby laser is a **three-level solid-state laser** in which a ruby rod (Al2O3 doped with about $0.05\%$ Cr$^{3+}$ ions) is placed inside a **helical flash lamp** inside a reflective cavity. The energy gap between the ground level and the pumping level is matched to the energy of the flash lamp photons.

**Working:**
1. On flashing, the ruby absorbs photons of wavelength about $694\ \text{nm}$... more precisely the flash lamp emits photons which raise the chromium ions from level $E_1$ to $E_3$ (a high unstable level).
2. Ions in $E_3$ decay quickly (in $10^{-8}$ s) to the **metastable** level $E_2$ by **spontaneous emission** of non-resonant photons, which are absorbed by the mirror coating so they do not stimulate emission.
3. Because the ions spend a long time (about $3 \times 10^{-3}$ s) in $E_2$, **population inversion** builds up.
4. An externally produced photon of wavelength $694.3\ \text{nm}$ (red) triggers **stimulated emission**: each incident photon reproduces itself and produces two identical photons. These photons multiply rapidly by repeated stimulation.
5. **Optical resonance:** The rod ends are silvered, one fully and the other partially. Photons bouncing repeatedly amplify the beam until $30\%$ of them emerge through the partially silvered end as a highly **collimated, monochromatic and coherent** red beam.

**Uses:**
1. **Surgery** — retina welding, kidney stone and cataract removal, brain tumour operations.
2. **Communication** — optical fibre transmission of signals in telephone and satellite links.
3. **Industry** — cutting, drilling and welding of very hard and thin materials, and aligning tunnel boring machines.
(Also: holograms, CD/DVD players, ranging, and printing.)
questions.knowledgeNote: A ruby laser uses a three-level pumping scheme, with population inversion in metastable levels giving stimulated red emission at 694 nm.

questions.question: State the Big Bang theory and the Hubble law. What evidence supports the expanding universe?
questions.solution:
**Big Bang theory:** The universe began as an extremely hot, dense point ~13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.

**Hubble's law:** v = H₀d — galaxies recede from us at velocities proportional to their distance. H₀ ≈ 67-70 km/s/Mpc.

**Evidence:**
1. Redshift of distant galaxies (Doppler shift)
2. Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) at 2.7 K
3. Abundance of light elements (H, He) matches Big Bang predictions
questions.knowledgeNote: Hubble's discovery (1929) showed that most galaxies are redshifted, meaning they are moving away — the universe is expanding.

questions.question: Explain why an object placed at the focus of a concave mirror produces an image at infinity, and state what happens for objects placed at C and between C and F.
questions.solution:
**Object at focus F ($u = f$):** Rays from any point on the object strike the mirror parallel to the principal axis. After reflection from a concave mirror, rays parallel to the principal axis pass through the focus and become **highly parallel**. So the reflected rays never meet at any finite point and the image is formed **at infinity**. This is used in searchlights, beam headlights and astronomical telescopes.

**Object at centre of curvature C ($u = 2f$):** Rays retrace their path, so the image is formed at C itself — **real, inverted and same size** ($m = -1$).

**Object between C and F ($f < u < 2f$):** The image forms **beyond $2f$** — **real, inverted and magnified** ($m > 1$), which is the principle of a projector.
questions.knowledgeNote: At the focus a concave mirror sends reflected rays parallel, giving an image at infinity; at C the image is same size.

questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position and magnification of the image and state its nature.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $u = -30\ \text{cm},\ f = -10\ \text{cm}$

**Step 2 — Mirror formula:**
$$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
$$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-30} = \frac{1}{-10}$$
$$\frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-3 + 1}{30} = -\frac{2}{30} = -\frac{1}{15}$$

**Step 3 — Image position:**
$$v = \mathbf{-15\ \text{cm}}$$
The image is 15 cm **in front of** the mirror (on the same side as the object).

**Step 4 — Magnification:**
$$m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-15}{-30} = \mathbf{-0.5}$$

**Step 5 — Nature:** $v < 0$ → image is **real**; $m < 0$ → **inverted**; $|m| = 0.5 < 1$ → **diminished**.
(The object is beyond $2f = 20$ cm, so the image is between $f$ and $2f$. ✓)
questions.knowledgeNote: With a concave mirror, an object beyond twice the focal length gives a real, inverted, diminished image between f and 2f.

questions.question: State the rules of the new Cartesian sign convention used for spherical mirrors.
questions.solution:
The new Cartesian sign convention has the following rules:

1. **Origin:** All distances are measured from the **pole (P)** of the mirror.
2. **Direction of incident light** is taken as **positive**. So distances measured against the incident light (behind the mirror) are negative.
3. **Principal axis:** Heights measured **above** the principal axis are positive and those **below** it are negative.
4. **Focal length:** For a **concave** mirror $f$ is **negative** (focus in front, on the reflected-light side); for a **convex** mirror $f$ is **positive**.
5. The mirror formula is written as
$$\boxed{\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}}\qquad \text{and} \qquad m = -\frac{v}{u}$$

Under this convention an object in front of a real mirror always has **negative** $u$.
questions.knowledgeNote: New Cartesian convention measures from pole, takes incident-light direction as positive, and gives f negative for concave mirrors.

questions.question: Differentiate between a concave mirror and a convex mirror.
questions.solution:
**Concave mirror:**
- It is **converging**; reflecting surface is on the **inner** side of the sphere.
- Focal length $f$ is **negative**.
- Image may be **real** or **virtual**, and may be inverted or erect, magnified or diminished.
- Magnification $m = -\dfrac{v}{u}$ can be greater or less than 1.
- The image lies in the **same region** as the object (mostly in front of the mirror).
- Used in headlights, projectors, dentist mirrors and reflecting telescopes.

**Convex mirror:**
- It is **diverging**; reflecting surface is on the **outer** side.
- Focal length $f$ is **positive**.
- Image is **always virtual, erect and diminished** ($0 < m < 1$).
- The image always lies **behind** the mirror and within the focus.
- Used as a rear-view mirror, in street lights and as a safety mirror.
questions.knowledgeNote: Concave mirrors are converging with negative focal length; convex mirrors are diverging with positive focal length.

questions.question: What is total internal reflection? State two conditions for it to occur.
questions.solution:

questions.question: The angle of deviation produced by a prism is: (a) always minimum when the ray passes symmetrically (b) always maximum when the ray passes symmetrically (c) independent of the angle of incidence (d) zero for a thin prism
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (a) always minimum when the ray passes symmetrically.**

The deviation varies with the angle of incidence. For a given prism, $\delta = i + e - A$. As $i$ is increased, $r_1$ increases, $r_2$ decreases and $e$ increases. At a certain value of $i$ we get $i = e$ (the ray passes **symmetrically** through the prism, so $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$), and at this position the deviation is **minimum**.
$$\boxed{i = e = \frac{A + \delta_{min}}{2}}$$
Hence options (b), (c) and (d) are all incorrect.
questions.knowledgeNote: Prism deviation is minimum when the ray passes symmetrically, so that i equals e and r1 equals r2.

questions.question: A prism of refracting angle 60° has a refractive index of 1.5 for the light used. If the angle of incidence is 40° and the internal angle of refraction at the first face is 30°, find the angle of emergence and the angle of deviation.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $A = 60^\circ,\ \mu = 1.5,\ i = 40^\circ,\ r_1 = 30^\circ$

**Step 2 — Internal angle at the second face:**
$$r_1 + r_2 = A \;\Rightarrow\; r_2 = 60^\circ - 30^\circ = 30^\circ$$

**Step 3 — Angle of emergence** using the law of refraction at the second face:
$$\mu = \frac{\sin e}{\sin r_2}$$
$$\sin e = \mu \sin r_2 = 1.5 \times \sin 30^\circ = 1.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75$$
$$e = \sin^{-1}(0.75) = \mathbf{48.6^\circ}$$

**Step 4 — Angle of deviation:**
$$\delta = i + e - A = 40^\circ + 48.6^\circ - 60^\circ$$
$$\boxed{\delta = \mathbf{28.6^\circ}}$$

**Note:** Since $i \ne e$ the prism is **not** at minimum deviation.
questions.knowledgeNote: Using mu equals sin e over sin r2 and delta equals i plus e minus A gives the emergence angle and deviation.

questions.question: What is a prism? Name its two types and define the angle of the prism.
questions.solution:
**Prism:** A prism is a transparent, refracting optical element with two plane refracting faces that are **not parallel** to each other, made of glass or other transparent material.

**Two types:**
1. **Triangular prism** — has two triangular bases and three rectangular refracting faces; used in spectroscopes.
2. **Rectangular (right-angled) prism** — used to deviate light through $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ (total internal reflection) or to invert an image.

**Angle of the prism (A):** The angle between the two refracting faces, measured inside the prism at the refracting edge, is called the angle of the prism.
$$A = r_1 + r_2$$
For an equilateral (Delisle's) prism, $A = 60^\circ$.
questions.knowledgeNote: A prism has two non-parallel refracting faces; its angle A equals the sum of internal refraction angles.

questions.question: Define minimum deviation and derive that the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base of the prism at minimum deviation.
questions.solution:
**Definition:** Minimum deviation is the **smallest angle of deviation** produced by a prism for a given pair of prism material and incident light, obtained when the ray passes symmetrically through the prism ($i = e$).

**Derivation:**
Let the ray travel through the two faces of the prism with internal angles $r_1$ and $r_2$ and internal deviations $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$.
$$\delta_1 = i - r_1, \qquad \delta_2 = e - r_2$$
$$\delta = i + e - (r_1 + r_2) = i + e - A$$

**Step 1 — The path inside the prism is the base of an isosceles triangle,** because the angle between the ray and the base is $90^\circ - r_1$ and also $90^\circ - r_2$.

**Step 2 — The deviation is minimum when the ray is symmetric,** i.e. $i = e$ and hence $r_1 = r_2$.

**Step 3 — Therefore:**
$$r_1 = r_2 = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2} = \frac{A}{2}$$
and
$$\boxed{i = e = \frac{A + \delta_{min}}{2}, \qquad \mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_{min}}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: At minimum deviation the internal ray is parallel to the base, so r1 equals r2 equals A over 2.

questions.question: Explain the energy band theory of solids. How does it differentiate metals, insulators, and semiconductors?
questions.solution:
In solids, atomic energy levels split into bands due to overlapping wavefunctions.

- **Metals:** Valence band overlaps conduction band (no gap), or conduction band is partially filled. Electrons move freely. Example: Cu, Ag.
- **Insulators:** Large forbidden gap (Eg > 3 eV) between valence and conduction bands. Very few electrons can cross. Example: Diamond, SiO₂.
- **Semiconductors:** Small forbidden gap (Eg ≈ 1 eV). At room temperature, some electrons cross to conduction band. Example: Si (Eg = 1.1 eV), Ge (Eg = 0.7 eV).
questions.knowledgeNote: The forbidden gap width determines conductivity. Intrinsic semiconductors: equal numbers of electrons and holes.

questions.question: What is an intrinsic semiconductor? Define electrons and holes as charge carriers.
questions.solution:
**Intrinsic semiconductor:** Pure semiconductor material without any impurities (e.g., pure silicon or germanium).

**Electron:** A negatively charged charge carrier promoted to the conduction band.
**Hole:** The positively charged vacancy left in the valence band when an electron leaves. Holes move in the direction of electric field.
questions.knowledgeNote: In an intrinsic semiconductor, nₑ = nₕ (equal number of electrons and holes).

questions.question: Differentiate between an elastic body and a plastic body.
questions.solution:
**Elastic body:**
- After the deforming force is removed, the body **regains its original size and shape** completely.
- Deformation is **reversible** and the limit of elasticity is not crossed.
- The restoring force lies within the elastic limit, so $F \propto x$ (Hooke's law).
- Property is measured by the **elastic modulus** (Young's modulus).
- Examples: steel, rubber (up to elastic limit), quartz, glass fibre.

**Plastic body:**
- After the deforming force is removed, the body **does not** regain its original shape and size; it keeps a **permanent deformation**.
- Deformation is **irreversible** and the elastic limit has been crossed.
- The limit of elasticity is small, e.g. $0.5\ \text{mm/m}$ for putty.
- Examples: putty, wet clay, wax, chewing gum, dough.

**Note:** Plastic deformation is essential in shaping metals by rolling, forging and bending.
questions.knowledgeNote: An elastic body regains its original shape after removing the deforming force; a plastic body keeps permanent deformation.

questions.question: Differentiate between a crystalline solid and an amorphous solid.
questions.solution:
**Crystalline solid:**
- Its particles (atoms, ions or molecules) are arranged in a **regular, orderly three-dimensional lattice** with a definite repeating pattern.
- Each crystal therefore has a **sharp, definite melting point** and a **fixed heat of fusion**.
- It has a **well-defined and fixed geometrical shape**, and definite cleavage directions, so it breaks along definite planes.
- Anisotropic: physical properties differ along different directions.
- Examples: quartz, diamond, common salt, ice, sugar.

**Amorphous solid:**
- Its particles are arranged **randomly and irregularly**, without any long-range order.
- It **softens gradually over a range of temperature** and has no sharp melting point.
- It has **no definite shape** and breaks along **irregular or curved** surfaces.
- Isotropic: physical properties are the same in all directions.
- Examples: glass, plastic, rubber, candle wax, gum, gelatin, pitch.
questions.knowledgeNote: Crystalline solids have ordered lattice, sharp melting point and fixed shape; amorphous solids are random and soften gradually.

questions.question: Define the coefficient of linear expansivity and write its formula and SI unit.
questions.solution:
**Definition:** The coefficient of linear expansivity $\alpha$ of a solid is defined as the **increase in length per unit original length per unit rise in temperature**.

**Formula:**
$$\alpha = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0 \Delta T} = \frac{L_T - L_0}{L_0 \Delta T}$$
where $\Delta L = L_T - L_0$ is the change in length.

**From the new length:** $L_T = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$

**SI unit:** $\text{K}^{-1}$ or $^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ (same, since a temperature interval of 1 K equals 1 degree Celsius). Dimensional formula: $\left[T^{-1}\right]$.

**Values:** Aluminium $\approx 23 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, brass $\approx 19 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, steel $\approx 11 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, glass $\approx 9 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Linear expansivity is the fractional increase in length per degree rise in temperature, with SI unit per kelvin.

questions.question: A metal rod of length 1 m at 20 degrees C is heated to 100 degrees C. If the coefficient of linear expansivity of the metal is $1.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, find the increase in length and the final length.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $L_0 = 1\ \text{m},\ T_1 = 20^\circ\text{C},\ T_2 = 100^\circ\text{C},\ \alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}$

**Step 2 — Change in temperature:**
$$\Delta T = T_2 - T_1 = 100 - 20 = 80\ \text{K}$$

**Step 3 — Increase in length:**
$$\Delta L = \alpha L_0 \Delta T = (1.2 \times 10^{-5})(1)(80) = 96 \times 10^{-5} = 9.6 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}$$
$$\boxed{\Delta L = \mathbf{9.6 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}} = \mathbf{0.96\ \text{mm}}}$$

**Step 4 — Final length:**
$$L_2 = L_0 + \Delta L = 1 + 9.6 \times 10^{-4}$$
$$\boxed{L_2 = \mathbf{1.00096\ \text{m}}$$

**Note:** The expansion is very small, which is why gaps are left in railway tracks and bridges.
questions.knowledgeNote: Expansion equals alpha times original length times temperature rise; for a one-metre rod it is a fraction of a millimetre.

questions.knowledgeNote: Work is a dot product (scalar); torque and angular momentum are cross products (vectors)

questions.question: Two forces P and Q are acting at a point. The magnitude of P is 10 N and Q is 20 N. If the angle between them is 60Â°, find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
questions.solution:
Magnitude: R = âˆš(PÂ² + QÂ² + 2PQ cos Î¸)
R = âˆš(10Â² + 20Â² + 2Ã—10Ã—20Ã—cos 60Â°) = âˆš(100 + 400 + 200) = âˆš700 = **26.46 N**

Direction: tan Î± = (Q sin Î¸)/(P + Q cos Î¸)
tan Î± = (20 sin 60Â°)/(10 + 20 cos 60Â°) = (20Ã—0.866)/(10+10) = 17.32/20 = 0.866
Î± = **40.89Â°** from P.
questions.knowledgeNote: Resultant magnitude formula: RÂ² = PÂ² + QÂ² + 2PQ cos Î¸. This is the law of cosines applied to vector addition.

questions.question: Add the vectors $(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})\ \text{m}$ and $(5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j})\ \text{m}$ and express the resultant in magnitude and direction form.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Add the corresponding components:**
$$\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}, \qquad \vec{B} = 5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}$$
$$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} = (3 + 5)\hat{i} + (4 - 12)\hat{j} = 8\hat{i} - 8\hat{j}$$

**Step 2 — Magnitude of the resultant:**
$$R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} = \sqrt{8^2 + (-8)^2} = \sqrt{64 + 64} = \sqrt{128}$$
$$\boxed{R = 8\sqrt{2} \approx \mathbf{11.3\ \text{m}}}$$

**Step 3 — Direction of the resultant:**
$$\tan\theta = \frac{R_y}{R_x} = \frac{-8}{8} = -1 \;\Rightarrow\; \theta = -45^\circ$$
$$\boxed{\theta = \mathbf{-45^\circ},\ \text{i.e. } 45^\circ \text{ south of east}}$$

The resultant lies in the fourth quadrant since $R_x > 0$ and $R_y < 0$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Vector components add algebraically; magnitude is the root of the sum of squared components and direction from the tangent ratio.

questions.question: Differentiate between scalar and vector quantities with examples.
questions.solution:
**Scalar quantity:** A physical quantity that has **magnitude only** and obeys the ordinary rules of algebra.
- Has **no direction**.
- Added by simple arithmetic.
- Examples: mass, time, temperature, distance, speed, work, energy, electric charge, volume.

**Vector quantity:** A physical quantity that has **both magnitude and direction** and obeys the law of vector (triangle or parallelogram) addition.
- Changes with direction.
- Cannot be added by simple arithmetic; its component form is $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$.
- Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, electric field, weight.

**Note:** Speed is the scalar counterpart of velocity, and mass is the scalar counterpart of weight.
questions.knowledgeNote: Scalars have magnitude only and add arithmetically; vectors have magnitude and direction and follow vector addition.

questions.question: State and prove the work-energy theorem for a constant force.
questions.solution:
**Work-energy theorem:** The work done by the net force on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

Proof: Let a constant force F act on a body of mass m, producing acceleration a. From vÂ² = uÂ² + 2as:
  W = FÂ·s = (ma)s = m(aÂ·s)
From vÂ² = uÂ² + 2as â†’ as = (vÂ²-uÂ²)/2
  W = m(vÂ²-uÂ²)/2 = Â½mvÂ² - Â½muÂ² = Î”KE

Thus, work done = change in kinetic energy. Proved. âœ“
questions.knowledgeNote: Work-energy theorem applies to ALL forces (conservative and non-conservative). KE = Â½mvÂ²

questions.question: A body of mass 4 kg is released from rest and falls freely through a height of 10 m. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ and find the kinetic energy and speed of the body just before striking the ground.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — By the law of conservation of energy,** the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy:
$$mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

**Step 2 — Kinetic energy:**
$$KE = mgh = 4 \times 9.8 \times 10 = 392\ \text{J}$$
$$\boxed{KE = \mathbf{392\ \text{J}}$$

**Step 3 — Speed:**
$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh \;\Rightarrow\; v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 10} = \sqrt{196}$$
$$\boxed{v = \mathbf{14\ \text{m/s}}}$$

**Step 4 — Check:** $\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 14^2 = 2 \times 196 = 392\ \text{J}$ ✓ (independent of mass, as expected for free fall).
questions.knowledgeNote: In free fall, mgh equals half mv squared, giving v equals square root of 2gh independent of mass.

questions.question: An electric motor has a power output of 2 kW. How much time will it take to lift a 500 kg mass through 20 m? (g = 10 m/sÂ²)
questions.solution:
Work done W = mgh = 500 Ã— 10 Ã— 20 = 100,000 J = 10âµ J

Power P = W/t â†’ t = W/P = 10âµ/2000 = **50 seconds**
questions.knowledgeNote: Power = Work/Time. 1 W = 1 J/s. 1 HP = 746 W

questions.question: A person of mass 60 kg climbs a staircase of vertical height 8 m in 20 s. Assuming $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, calculate the power developed by the person.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Given:** $m = 60\ \text{kg},\ h = 8\ \text{m},\ t = 20\ \text{s}$

**Step 2 — Work done against gravity** (the useful work in climbing):
$$W = mgh = 60 \times 9.8 \times 8$$
$$W = 4704\ \text{J}$$

**Step 3 — Power developed:**
$$P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{mgh}{t} = \frac{60 \times 9.8 \times 8}{20}$$
$$\boxed{P = \mathbf{235.2\ \text{W}}\approx \mathbf{235\ \text{W}}$$

**Note:** This is the useful mechanical power only; a human body is about $20\%$ efficient, so the metabolic power consumed is much higher.
questions.knowledgeNote: Power developed while lifting a body equals mgh divided by time, which here is 235 watts.

questions.question: Define work, energy and power with their SI units.
questions.solution:
**Work:** The work done by a force $F$ acting on a body through a displacement $s$ in the direction of the force is
$$W = Fs\cos\theta = F \cdot s$$
Work is a **scalar** and its SI unit is the **joule (J)**, where $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$.

**Energy:** The capacity of a body to do work is called energy. Its SI unit is also the **joule**, and $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m} = 1\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}$. Energy is also a scalar and its dimensions are $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.

**Power:** The rate of doing work is called power.
$$P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{F s}{t} = F v$$
Its SI unit is the **watt (W)**, where $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1} = 1\ \text{V A}$.
questions.knowledgeNote: Work is force times displacement, energy is the capacity to do work, and power is the rate of doing work.

questions.question: State and explain the work-energy theorem.
questions.solution:
**Statement:** The work done by the resultant (net) force on a body is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
$$\boxed{W_{net} = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2}$$

**Explanation:**
Let a net force $F$ acting on a body of mass $m$ produce an acceleration $a$, so it moves from velocity $u$ to $v$ in time $t$ and covers a distance $s$.
**Step 1 — Work done:**
$$W = Fs = mat = m\left(\frac{v - u}{t}\right)t = m(v - u)$$
$$
**Step 2 — Change in kinetic energy:**
$$\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(v - u)(v + u)$$

**Step 3 — From Newton's second law** $F = ma = m\left(\dfrac{v - u}{t}\right)$, we get $mt = m(v - u)$, so
$$\boxed{W = m(v-u) = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2) = \Delta K}$$

If the net work is zero, the speed stays constant, which explains why a body moves uniformly without net force.
questions.knowledgeNote: The work-energy theorem states net work done equals the change in kinetic energy of the body.

questions.question: Define mole. Calculate the number of moles in 44 g of CO₂.
questions.solution:
A **mole** is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of C-12 (6.022 × 10²³ particles).

Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 32 = 44 g mol⁻¹.

n = mass/molar mass = 44/44 = **1 mole**.

questions.question: State Avogadro's law. What volume does 0.25 mole of a gas occupy at STP?
questions.solution:
**Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

At STP, 1 mole occupies 22.4 L ⇒ 0.25 mole occupies 0.25 × 22.4 = **5.6 L**.

questions.question: An organic compound contains 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen and 53.33% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16).
questions.solution:
Divide each % by atomic mass: C = 40/12 = 3.33; H = 6.67/1 = 6.67; O = 53.33/16 = 3.33.

Divide by the smallest (3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.

**Empirical formula = CH₂O**.

questions.question: Distinguish between empirical and molecular formula with an example.
questions.solution:
The **empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound; the **molecular formula** gives the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

Example — benzene: molecular formula C₆H₆, empirical formula CH.

questions.question: State Dalton's atomic theory. What are its main drawbacks?
questions.solution:
**Dalton's postulates:** matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties; atoms of different elements differ; compounds form by combination of atoms in simple whole-number ratios.

**Drawbacks:** atom is divisible (electrons, protons, neutrons exist); isotopes of an element have different masses; it cannot explain complex ratios, isotopy or the nature of bonding.

questions.question: Write the electronic configuration of Fe (Z = 26) and Cr (Z = 24) and explain any anomaly.
questions.solution:
**Fe:** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶.

**Cr:** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹ 3d⁵.

**Anomaly:** chromium takes one electron from 4s into 3d to give a half-filled 3d⁵ configuration, which has extra stability due to symmetrical distribution and maximum exchange energy.

questions.question: Why is ionisation energy of nitrogen greater than that of oxygen?
questions.solution: Nitrogen has a half-filled stable 2p³ configuration, which requires more energy to remove an electron. In oxygen, removing one electron gives a more stable half-filled 2p³ arrangement, so less energy is needed — hence IE(N) > IE(O).

questions.question: Define hybridisation. What is the shape and bond angle of NH₃?
questions.solution:
**Hybridisation** is the intermixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy to form an equal number of identical hybrid orbitals.

In NH₃ nitrogen is sp³ hybridised: one lone pair + three N–H bonds ⇒ **pyramidal shape**, bond angle **107°** (compressed from 109.5° by the lone pair).

questions.question: What is a limiting reagent? 2 g of hydrogen reacts with 32 g of oxygen to form water. Identify the limiting reagent and the mass of water formed.
questions.solution:
A **limiting reagent** is the reactant completely consumed in the reaction and which therefore limits the amount of product.

Reaction: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (4 g H₂ reacts with 32 g O₂).

Here only 2 g H₂ is available ⇒ H₂ is the **limiting reagent**.

4 g H₂ → 36 g H₂O, so 2 g H₂ → **18 g of water**.

questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles' law. Write the ideal gas equation.
questions.solution:
**Boyle's law:** at constant temperature the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (V ∝ 1/P).

**Charles' law:** at constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V ∝ T).

Combining with Avogadro's law gives the **ideal gas equation: PV = nRT**.

questions.question: Define oxidation number. Find the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation number** is the charge an atom would have if electrons were transferred completely to the more electronegative atom.

In H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 ⇒ S = +8 − 2 = **+6**.

questions.question: Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour?
questions.solution: At high pressure the volume occupied by gas molecules is no longer negligible compared with the container volume; at low temperature intermolecular attractions become significant. Both effects make PV ≠ nRT — hence real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature.

questions.question: Explain the shape of the water molecule using VSEPR theory.
questions.solution:
In H₂O, oxygen is sp³ hybridised with **two bond pairs and two lone pairs**.

According to VSEPR, lone pair–lone pair repulsion is greater than lone pair–bond pair repulsion, which compresses the tetrahedral angle from 109.5° to about **104.5°**.

Hence the shape of H₂O is **bent (angular or V-shaped)**.

questions.question: Define ionisation energy. Why does it increase across a period?
questions.solution:
**Ionisation energy** is the minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

Across a period nuclear charge increases while the shell number stays the same, so electrons are held more strongly — more energy is needed to remove them. Hence IE increases across a period.

questions.question: What are isotopes? Give one example.
questions.solution:
**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).

Example: protium (¹₁H), deuterium (²₁H) and tritium (³₁H) — isotopes of hydrogen; also ¹²C and ¹⁴C.

questions.question: Write a short note on Graham's law of diffusion.
questions.solution:
**Graham's law:** at constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass: r ∝ 1/√M, so r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).

Lighter gases diffuse faster — e.g. hydrogen diffuses about four times faster than oxygen.

questions.question: State Le Chatelier's principle. Predict the effect of increasing pressure on N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
questions.solution:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that minimises the disturbance.

For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ there are 4 moles of gas on the left and only 2 on the right. Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium **towards the right (more ammonia)**, since fewer gas molecules means lower pressure.

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution.
questions.solution:
HCl is a strong acid and dissociates completely: [H⁺] = 0.001 = 10⁻³ M.

pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(10⁻³) = **3**.

questions.question: What is a coordinate (dative) bond? Give an example.
questions.solution:
A **coordinate bond** is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the two bonded atoms (the donor), the other being the acceptor.

Example: NH₄⁺ — nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺; also H₃O⁺.

questions.question: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation** is the loss of electrons by an atom/ion (increase in oxidation number). **Reduction** is the gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number).

Example: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

questions.question: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and give its significance.
questions.solution:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle:** it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the position and the momentum of a moving microscopic particle.

Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π.

**Significance:** it rules out fixed orbits for electrons (contradicting Bohr) and leads to the concept of orbitals — regions of probability of finding the electron.

questions.question: What is the de Broglie equation? Calculate the wavelength of an electron moving at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
questions.solution:
The **de Broglie equation** λ = h/mv relates the wave nature to the particle nature of matter.

λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶)

= 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9.1 × 10⁻²⁵ ≈ **7.28 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.728 nm**.

questions.question: Why are noble gases chemically inert? Explain with reference to their electronic configuration.
questions.solution: Noble gases have completely filled outermost shells (ns² np⁶, except helium 1s²), giving maximum stability. They neither need to lose nor gain electrons, so they have high ionisation energy, almost zero electron affinity and very low reactivity.

questions.question: Distinguish between sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds.
questions.solution:
**Sigma bond:** formed by head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals; stronger; free rotation possible; only one σ bond between two atoms.

**Pi bond:** formed by sidewise (lateral) overlap of p-orbitals; weaker; rotation restricted; always present along with a σ bond (in double/triple bonds).

questions.question: Define molarity. Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH in 500 mL of solution.
questions.solution:
**Molarity (M)** is the number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of solution.

Moles of NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 500 mL = 0.5 L.

M = 0.1 / 0.5 = **0.2 M**.

questions.question: What is sp³ hybridisation? Explain the structure of methane using it.
questions.solution:
In **sp³ hybridisation** one s orbital and three p orbitals of comparable energy mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally at 109°28′.

In CH₄, carbon's one 2s electron is promoted to 2p, giving four unpaired electrons which hybridise into four sp³ orbitals; each overlaps with a hydrogen 1s orbital forming four identical C–H bonds — hence CH₄ is **tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5°**.

questions.question: State Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.
questions.solution:
**Pauli exclusion principle:** no two electrons in the same atom can have all four quantum numbers identical — an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

**Hund's rule:** electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins before pairing begins, because this arrangement has maximum stability (maximum multiplicity).

questions.question: Why is BF₃ non-polar while NF₃ is polar?
questions.solution:
BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical: the three B–F bond dipoles cancel exactly ⇒ net dipole moment is zero ⇒ **non-polar**.

NF₃ is pyramidal (lone pair on N): the N–F bond dipoles do not cancel ⇒ net dipole moment exists ⇒ **polar**.

questions.question: What is a functional group? Write the general formula of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
questions.solution:
A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic chemical properties of an organic compound (e.g. –OH, –CHO, –COOH).

Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ; Alkynes: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

questions.question: Define isomerism. Draw the chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ and name them.
questions.solution:
**Isomerism** is the phenomenon in which compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements (and hence different properties).

Chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ (pentane):
1. **n-pentane** — CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃
2. **isopentane (2-methylbutane)** — (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH₃
3. **neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane)** — C(CH₃)₄

questions.question: Explain why the bond angle in NH₃ is greater than that in H₂O.
questions.solution:
